title: Assessment Without Appraisal
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Assessment Without Appraisal

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. This research received no external funding.
declarations.funderStatement: None. This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Wealth, property and estate taxes need current values for assets that rarely trade, and today they rest on appraisal: costly, contestable and systematically wrong. This paper presents an assessment system with no appraisals and no required filing. Owners keep their own values current on a register and have reason to keep them close to the market price. The register moves only on evidence that is costly to fake, and a companion paper shows that, within its axioms, the weights given to that evidence are the only ones that survive free collusion. The valuation is, to our knowledge, the first self-assessment scheme that tests values against the market in both directions, never forces a sale, and works for shared as well as sole-owned assets (several share classes need a conversion model, left open). Understatement is limited by what outsiders can know and by the cost of checking, and the limit tightens as assets grow. Owners pay in cash, in shares if listed, or by capped deferral, which smooths the need for cash but cannot remove it. Applications include wealth and property taxes, estate valuation, and private-company share pricing in place of 409A appraisals.

title: The Same Data Can Help or Harm: Learner-State-Dependent Data Value in Emotion Recognition
affiliations: Kansai University

detail.title: The Same Data Can Help or Harm: Learner-State-Dependent Data Value in Emotion Recognition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Neural classifiers are increasingly trained with auxiliary data, such as texts generated by large language models (LLMs), and the value of such data is usually treated as a fixed property of the data. In emotion recognition, where labels are subjective and naturally soft, it is unclear whether this assumption holds. In this study, we analyze how the value of the same auxiliary data depends on the learner. We define a real-data exchange rate, which expresses the gain of an auxiliary pool in units of real examples at each real-data size of the learner. We then design an entropy-matched intervention that changes only the direction of soft targets while the text, the argmax label, and the mean entropy are fixed, and a teacher trained on the same real data separates this effect from distillation. We also cross the text source with the label direction at matched perturbation strength, and we test static, first-order, and trajectory-based predictors of value on two emotion corpora in English and Japanese. The same generated data helped small learners and harmed large ones. Soft mass directed toward a teacher reduced or removed this harm, whereas other directions at the same entropy did not. A wrong direction cost more on generated texts than on real texts. No static or first-order quantity ranked the harm reliably, whereas a few actual updates did, and the sign of the value differed between metrics in some conditions. These results indicate that, in emotion recognition, data value is a relation between the data, the learner state, and the objective rather than a property of the data alone.

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not obtained before data collection. The study protocol, questionnaire, and data-handling procedures were reviewed retrospectively and approved by the Ethics Review Committee for Research Involving Human Subjects of the Center for Global Communications, International University of Japan, on 3 April 2026 (approval number GE25001). The study followed the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki regarding voluntary participation, informed consent, and confidentiality. At the start of the online survey, respondents were informed that the survey was conducted for research by the Center for Global Communications, that responses were anonymous and would be used only for research, that results might be published in a form that did not identify respondents, and that participation was voluntary and declining would carry no disadvantage. Respondents gave informed consent, including consent to the publication of anonymised results, by proceeding to answer the questionnaire.

detail.abstract: This study examined how closely self-reported generative AI (GenAI) literacy corresponds to tested knowledge, focusing on item content and respondents’ current use of GenAI. Using an online survey of 5,000 adults aged 20–69 in Japan, we compared a 14-item self-report scale with a ten-item scored test. Correlations with the test varied widely with item content, from .370 for understanding of mechanisms and risks to .084 for basic use, and the total score fell between them at .225. Among the 2,626 respondents who did not currently use GenAI, the corresponding correlations were .265 and −.127. Associations with technology acceptance constructs also differed depending on whether literacy was measured by the test or by self-report, and on model specification. The findings indicate that a total self-report score should not be treated as a proxy for tested knowledge without considering item content, the coverage of the criterion test and respondents’ use status.

detail.abstract: America's exorbitant privilege is traditionally attributed to foreign investors willing to pay a premium for U.S. Treasuries. This paper documents a shift in the demand driving that premium. The comovement between foreign Treasury holdings and the Treasury covered interest parity (CIP) basis turns significantly negative around 2013, suggesting a growing role for domestic demand. This shift is concentrated in the Treasury-specific component of the basis and is associated with the declining role of foreign official investors and banks and the increasing importance of U.S. banks. Bank-level evidence links this change to post-crisis liquidity regulation, particularly the Liquidity Coverage Ratio. A two-country model shows that regulatory demand can generate this pattern and that a premium increasingly driven by domestic banks need not deliver greater welfare benefits to the United States. These findings suggest that America's exorbitant privilege is becoming increasingly domestic in origin, with diminishing external benefits.

title: Rising Obsolescence:  Measuring Obsolescence and its Effect on R&D
affiliations: Technology & Policy Research Initiative, BU School of Law, Singapore Management University and Northeastern Univeristy

detail.title: Rising Obsolescence:  Measuring Obsolescence and its Effect on R&D

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Technology and Policy Research Initiative at Boston University

affiliations.preferred_name: Technology & Policy Research Initiative, BU School of Law

detail.abstract: Obsolescence is a central variable for understanding innovation. It affects firm decisions to invest in R&D and to adopt new technologies; it affects the calculation of R&D's contribution to productivity growth. Yet obsolescence rates are typically assumed to be constant over time and uniform across firms even in technologically dynamic sectors. This paper explores three measures of variable obsolescence based on patent citations (Ma 2025), patent renewals, and firm responses to rivals' R&D. All three measures are correlated, they all rose sharply since 2005, and they vary strongly with rivals' R&D. Obsolescence significantly affects firm R&D spending. And rising obsolescence reduces R&D's contribution to productivity growth, possibly accounting for a significant share of the productivity slowdown after 2005.

reference: Forthcoming in Stanford Journal of Law, Economics & Business, Volume 31
title: Investor Communication and Say-on-Pay
affiliations: Duke University School of Law

detail.title: Investor Communication and Say-on-Pay

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: N/a.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Stanford Journal of Law, Economics & Business, Volume 31

detail.abstract:
It is well-understood that, on the margin, collective action problems and federal securities law disincentive communication among public-company investors. Activist shareholders who wish to hold corporate insiders to account, however, must rely on support from other investors to effect change. At the same time, Congress has recently mandated that all public companies give investors a nonbinding vote on executive pay. Yet few have considered whether such votes communicate information on investor satisfaction with incumbents to activists. That consequence-intended or not-could carry significant implications for corporate governance. 

In this Article, I show that the federal say-on-pay mandate provides a channel for institutional investors to communicate openness to an activist engagement. In particular, I exploit a unique feature of the say-on-pay regulatory regime to show that holding such a vote increases the odds of future activism. I then test implications of this finding, providing evidence that the results of those votes correlate with the likelihood of future activism, and that the say-on-pay voting system facilitates successful outcomes for activists. I conclude that those who favor shareholder voting as a corporate governance mechanism should carefully consider the effects of such votes on investor communication when evaluating such policies.

reference: Forthcoming in University of Miami Law Review, Volume 81
title: Corporate Silence
affiliations: Duke University School of Law

detail.title: Corporate Silence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: N/a.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in University of Miami Law Review, Volume 81

detail.abstract:
This Article addresses the phenomenon of corporate silence, which I take to be the absence of expected corporate action. While many other areas of law recognize the relationship between action and nonaction, the lion's share of the existing empirical corporate literature focuses on the action. This is understandable: one typically imagines the "cause" in cause-and-effect as a transpired action, and identifying nonaction may be difficult in practice. But difficulties in conceptualizing or capturing instances of nonaction do not make the phenomenon any less deserving of attention. 

With this observation in hand, I extend the traditional event study methodology to examine the process by which the market incorporates information contained in nonaction. In so doing, I offer a means to test whether the absence of an expected action conveys economically valuable information. 

I then provide empirical evidence of the informative nature of nonaction in the context of stock trades-or more specifically, the absence of expected stock trades-by corporate insiders. Using a simple model of expected trading activity, I show that stocks tend to underperform when insiders abstain from expected buying activity, and tend to outperform when insiders abstain from expected selling activity. I test implications of this finding, providing evidence that the effect strengthens with prolonged silence, and that silence can be used to predict good and bad news about the firm, as well as mergers and acquisitions activity. I discuss the consequences of these findings not only for the law of insider trading and the study of markets, but also for the broader policy choice between disclosure and direct regulation. In particular, disclosure and direct regulation are complements, rather than substitutes, and the effects of corporate silence must be considered in any analysis of the tradeoffs between them.

detail.abstract:
Systematically buying 1-day Nasdaq-100 Index (NDX) straddles and strangles generated cumulative profits from 2023 through the third quarter of 2026, while systematically selling either structure produced losses in every annual period examined. These results challenge the assumption that consistently selling short-dated options necessarily offers an advantage over buying them.

The study compares daily straddle and strangle trades held through expiration, using midpoint option prices and a 2.00-point allowance per structure for slippage and commissions. Buying one straddle each day generated cumulative profits of 3,796 index points, compared with 3,497 points for one strangle. Although their cumulative profits were similar, the strategies offered different trade-offs: straddles won more frequently and produced larger maximum daily gains, while strangles required substantially less premium and experienced smaller maximum daily losses.

Position sizing materially changed the comparison. Because a strangle typically cost approximately one-third as much as a straddle, purchasing three strangles provided an approximate comparison at similar initial premium outlays. This approach generated substantially greater cumulative profits than buying one straddle but also produced larger worst-day losses and a significant drawdown. The findings show that strategy selection depends on capital commitment and tolerance for losses as well as cumulative profitability, with outcomes sensitive to market conditions and trading costs.

detail.abstract: Do political connections create barriers to entry in financial intermediation? Exploiting an unexpected weakening of political ties between private equity firms and public officials induced by the SEC's pay-to-play rule in 2010, we find that more exposed public pensions become more likely to invest in first-time funds. A one-standard-deviation increase in exposure raises this probability by two percentage points. Political contributions decline disproportionately among managers with existing pension relationships, and exposed pensions reduce reinvestment with existing managers. Investment performance also improves. These findings suggest that restricting political connections facilitates entry and improves public pension capital allocation.

title: Does AI Retain Physicians? A Seniority Gradient and Expertise Reallocation in Hospitals
affiliations: Boston University and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Does AI Retain Physicians? A Seniority Gradient and Expertise Reallocation in Hospitals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing financial or personal interests.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly adopted in hospital information systems and now performs part of physicians' work. Amid physician shortages, AI has been proposed as a strategy to retain physicians, but longitudinal evidence on whether it does is lacking. We quantify the effect of AI exposure on physician exit at three levels of seniority. From a census of technology installations in U.S. hospitals, we identify 94 AI-enabled products for clinical decision support and link them to the career histories of 288,661 physicians in 3,144 hospitals, observed in 1.92 million position-years from 2015 to 2025, and to the 362 tasks of 20 physician occupations. We measure the breadth of AI exposure as the share of an occupation's tasks that the hospital's installed products can perform and estimate stratified Cox models of exit with hospital-by-year and occupation-by-year fixed effects. We find three results. First, decision-support AI retains junior physicians. Each 10 percentage points of tasks covered lowers their annual exit hazard by 5.8%, and at the 90th percentile of exposure their five-year retention is 4.2 percentage points higher than among unexposed peers. Second, the effect of exposure on exit rises by 7.2% with each step up in seniority, and exposed senior physicians are more likely to leave, with five-year retention 5.9 percentage points lower at the 90th percentile. Third, the gradient is specific to decision-support AI and arises from the tools that inform the choice and delivery of treatment. AI tools designed to support hospital administration show no significant gradient. These effects are consistent with a reallocation of clinical expertise within and across hospitals. Within hospitals, exposed senior physicians bill fewer complex office visits. Across hospitals, exposed senior physicians are more likely to move to other hospitals and gain in estimated pay, and exposed junior physicians are less likely to move out of hospitals. Hospitals should evaluate AI as a retention strategy by physician seniority and by the clinical decisions it can inform.

title: The Second Bride in the Bath: A Roadmap for a Monopolization Case Against Google in AI
affiliations: Yale University - Law School, Yale School of Management and Yale Law School

detail.title: The Second Bride in the Bath: A Roadmap for a Monopolization Case Against Google in AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
AI is widely considered to be the first serious competitive threat to Google's search monopoly in decades. This Article argues that the same disruption may instead allow Google to build its next monopoly. Google enters the AI transition with an extraordinary set of structural advantages: a monopoly in general search, control of one of the two primary mobile operating systems, a suite of applications used by billions of consumers, vast proprietary data, and a presence across nearly every layer of the AI stack including chips, cloud, foundation models, applications, and distribution. Google is now deploying those assets to distribute Gemini, privilege it over rival AI assistants, and absorb the competitive threat posed by generative AI into its existing ecosystem. 

This Article develops a roadmap for applying § 2 of the Sherman Act to that conduct. It advances three related theories. First, Google is unlawfully maintaining its search monopoly by using defaults, distribution, data advantages, and product integration to prevent rivals from developing into effective substitutes for search. The strategy closely resembles the conduct condemned in Microsoft: confronted with a technology capable of displacing the incumbent platform, the monopolist embeds that technology into its own product while denying independent rivals the distribution and scale necessary to mature into a competitive threat. Second, Google is attempting to monopolize the emerging market for consumer AI assistants. Its control of Android, privileged integration of Gemini across Google's applications, agreements with device manufacturers, and partnership with Apple give Google control over critical channels through which AI assistants reach consumers. Third, these integrations may constitute unlawful tying where Google uses products over which it possesses market power to secure distribution for Gemini while denying rivals equivalent access. 

The Article's central contribution is to analyze these practices not in isolation, but as part of an ecosystem-wide strategy informed by Google's prior conduct. Google has already been found liable for unlawful monopolization in the search and ad technology markets in the U.S. Now, at the outset of a new technological cycle, it is deploying familiar exclusionary mechanisms including defaults, control over distribution, privileged interoperability, and ecosystem leverage. This history matters in assessing both the likely competitive effects of Google's conduct and the risk that these practices will combine to entrench market power. The Article concludes that the nascency of AI markets is a reason for timely enforcement, not delay. Digital markets shaped by defaults, data feedback loops, network effects, and ecosystem advantages can tip rapidly, after which effective remedies may be difficult or impossible. In such markets, early enforcement is timely enforcement: intervention while competition remains viable may be the only realistic opportunity to preserve it.

detail.abstract: How stable is the relationship between oil prices and currency volatility? We study eight advanced economies over March 2000-December 2024 using monthly volatility constructed from daily exchange rates. A local-linear fixed-effects model allows associations with real oil price changes, oil variability, the VIX and US yield changes to evolve over time. Dependence-aware simultaneous bands distinguish changing point estimates from supported sign changes. The common oil coefficient crosses zero, but its baseline band includes zero throughout the interior and accommodates a constant coefficient. Alternative benchmarks and conditioning sets reveal some negative episodes without establishing a positive-to-negative reversal. The VIX association is more clearly positive and time-varying, and country oil slopes depart from their average. Generalized responses from a monthly global-variable system indicate short-horizon financial-risk comovement; oil responses are less precise and sensitive to contemporaneous allocation. Matched-sample local projections provide no stronger oil-sign evidence. The results favour a conditional, currency-specific interpretation of oil-FX linkages, with a clear distinction between contemporaneous associations and joint market dynamics.

title: The Vanishing Worksite: The Collapse Of Place In Employment Law
affiliations: University of Colorado Law School

detail.title: The Vanishing Worksite: The Collapse Of Place In Employment Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
In the modern economy, the physical worksite is increasingly irrelevant for much employment. Nonetheless, core employment laws still focus on worksites and locations. 

This Article challenges the continued reliance on physical place for accessing important employment protections. It argues that place functions primarily as a proxy for other regulatory concerns: the degree of employer control and direction over workers, Congress's judgment about the appropriate scope of statutory coverage, and the interests of communities affected by employment decisions. While formalistic place-based requirements may have once offered an administrable bright line, in today's economy that line has blurred, resulting in ambiguity, arbitrary distinctions among similarly situated workers, and the narrowing of employment protections. 

Seventeen million workers in the United States work fully remotely, and one in five workers work remotely some of the time. In addition to traditionally mobile workers, such as salespeople, many app-based workers lack a fixed place of work. At the same time, the fissuring of the workplace means many workers are subcontracted to shifting physical locations. 

The connection between work and place has weakened, yet place-based requirements remain embedded in major employment statutes. These include the Equal Pay Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, and the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification ("WARN") Act, which has gained renewed significance amid concerns about AI-driven displacement. Together, these statutes cover more than 100 million workers. 

Drawing on the development of other legal doctrines (including contract, personal jurisdiction, and tax law), which have broadened or abandoned formal place-based tests, this Article calls for a similar rethinking in employment law.

detail.abstract: This chapter explores the complex relationship between intellectual property (IP) and sustainability, two concepts that increasingly intersect in contemporary society but remain difficult to reconcile. While IP law is traditionally characterized by exclusivity, territoriality, proprietary rights, linear value creation, and technological specificity, sustainability emphasizes inclusiveness, shared resources, global responsibility, circularity, and long-term social and environmental benefits. The chapter argues that IP can both facilitate and hinder sustainable practices, depending on the relevant rights, uses, and legal mechanisms. As a timely case study, the chapter examines upcycling and identifies three key symptoms that make the identification of possible pathways for reconciling IP protection with sustainability, advancing environmentally and socially responsible creative practices, and eliminate the sustainability crisis of IP law complicated. These symptoms include the overprotection of IP rights and limited support of socially beneficial sustainable solutions; the asymmetric nature of IP overlaps, namely, the horizontal protection of IP rights and the lack of horizontal application of exceptions and limitations thereto; finally, the tensions of fundamental rights and principles of opposing stakeholders. Last, the chapter proposes legislative reforms, constructive legal interpretation, and soft law solutions to better align IP with the circular economy.

title: Menopause And Legal Silence
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law, University of Virginia School of Law and Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Menopause And Legal Silence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

affiliations.org_name: University of Virginia (UVA) - School of Law, Faculty
affiliations.preferred_name: University of Virginia School of Law

detail.abstract:
Menopause is a predictable and biological inevitability experienced by approximately half the workforce, but it is largely invisible in U.S. law.  In this chapter written for The Routledge Handbook of the Anthropology of Menstruation (2027), the authors argue that this absence has consequences. In failing to address menopause, the law perpetuates ideas that some bodies at midlife are insignificant or shameful, given that the workplace is designed around a static “ideal worker.”

Menopause is not mentioned specifically in federal anti-discrimination law. Practically speaking, symptoms associated with menopause may give rise to a claim under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or even Title VII if they are severe enough to be classified as a disability or if a worker experiences discrimination against because of their sex. However, case law such as Sipple v Crossmark and Coleman v Bobby Dodd Institute shows that existing law fails to provide a meaningful remedy when adverse employment action is taken on account of a worker's menopausal symptoms.

Through the anthropological lenses of biocultural embodiment, the “mindful body”, biomedical decline, and structural stigma, this chapter explores why menopause is being ignored by law. It compares the U.S. legal landscape to the United Kingdom's. Court there have started to recognize that menopause can be a condition that require gender-aware responses.  Reference is also made to Japan, a country that offers menstruation leave for employees, but the benefit is not commonly accessed. We will also look at states and municipalities who have recently tried to incorporate menopause into their legislation. A survey of state-level menopause-equity reforms in the U.S. suggest that reform is possible, but more needs to be done to allow workers to thrive in their careers while experiencing menopause. Workplace change, regulations, increased healthcare access, and the commercialization of “menopause” are relevant to reform. The chapter includes lessons from the menstrual equity movement, as well.

detail.abstract: This study explores how Sri Lankan legal framework impacts the freedom of expression on social media, amidst ethnic and religious sensitivities. As a multicultural and multireligious society with a history of complex ethnic tensions and political conflict, Sri Lanka has faced challenges when regulating social media while ensuring national security and public order as grounds to restrict freedom of expression. So, this research identifies how broad and ambiguous legal provisions, in conjunction with selective enforcement of laws, and limited judicial oversight effects the freedom of expression in digital space. By using a comparative approach, this study analyses how India has implemented more structured and transparent mechanisms to regulate freedom of expression in social media, while having similar problems that Sri Lanka faced as a south Asian country with a diverse multicultural and multi-religious society. Finally, by evaluating legal practices and legal enforcements of Sri Lanka and India. the research highlights the need of more balanced model that protects freedom of expression while managing online content responsibly to maintain the balance between responsible digital regulation and freedom of expression in Sri Lanka. The findings emphasize the importance of critically evaluating the legal practices, enforcement patterns, and practical challenges present in both Sri Lanka and India, while also, focusing on the importance of accountability, and inclusive policy making to maintain a social media regulation legal framework that upholds freedom of expression while maintaining appropriate controls on social media. For that the study used India as a comparator to draw insights and recommendations for improving regulatory practices in Sri Lanka.

detail.abstract:
This report examines global legislative and regulatory responses to misinformation, disinformation, and mal-information (MDM) between 1995 and 2025. Drawing on an expanded and updated dataset of 409 coded regulatory and policy entries, including hard and soft law, policy measures, and proposed or draft instruments, it analyses their growth, geographic distribution, substantive focuses, and regulatory designs, which represent the various approaches taken against MDM, as well as early evidence of their implementation.

The central finding is sustained and accelerating regulatory growth. Annual activity increased from 11 instruments in 2016 to 46 in 2023, 67 in 2024, and 71 in 2025. The number of instruments currently in force has reached 282, despite 34 measures having been repealed, withdrawn, or judicially invalidated. This growth has also been accompanied by a shift in regulatory focus. Earlier measures relied heavily on broad prohibitions of “false information,” whereas more recent measures increasingly target specific harms, including deepfakes, election interference, non-consensual intimate imagery, and child safety. Regulatory responsibility is also increasingly being placed on platforms rather than solely on individual creators and users.

The report classifies these responses into six regulatory models: truth-policing, criminal harm prevention, platform systems governance, victim-centred rights and remedies, provenance regulation, and resilience-based approaches. Criminal harm prevention and truth-policing remain among the most common. Since 2023, however, new regulatory activity has increasingly concentrated on platform systems governance, victim-centred remedies, and provenance regulation. This indicates a broader shift from assessing the truthfulness of individual claims towards regulating the systems, technologies, and actors through which information is created and distributed.

The report also moves beyond the formal content of legislation to examine how regulation operates in practice. Illustrative cases, such as Singapore’s POFMA, the European Union’s Digital Services Act, South Korea’s deepfake-crime amendments, and the judicial invalidation of truth-determination measures in India and Mongolia, show that enforcement outcomes, unintended consequences, and institutional capacity can differ substantially from what legislation provides on paper. The evidence suggests that regulatory effectiveness depends not only on the scope of formal legal powers, but also on the capacity of institutions to implement and enforce them consistently.

The report concludes by identifying priorities for the future. These include converting unstructured information on informational harms, safeguards and institutional arrangements into comparable variables; systematically recording implementation, enforcement, and judicial outcomes alongside formal legal powers; extending the analysis of factors associated with regulatory design and implementation; expanding the use of non-English-language sources; and maintaining the dataset through annual updates, with substantive updates planned for mid-2027 and mid-2028.

detail.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence opens the prospect of reconfiguring how audit firms organize work and create assurance value. This paper introduces the Agentic Audit Firm, integrating Porter's value-chain perspective with a digital workforce of specialized AI agents. We instantiate this vision in a five-agent prototype that performs journal entry testing on real-world accounting records, from transaction analysis through review and reporting. We evaluate four multi-agent audit teams with contrasting preparation practices and review policies across six dimensions: expertise, independence, evidence, methodology, coordination, and review placement. Our initial findings reveal that, even with identical model assignments, teams differed in how well they maintained their risk ratings in the face of misleading journal entry descriptions and how often they followed up on procedures that flagged many entries. By making alternative team configurations executable and their outcomes comparable, the study establishes a foundation for self-improving agentic audit firms in which evaluated experience informs the organization of future assurance work.

detail.abstract:
Today, more than half of the world’s research authors are based in low- and middle-income countries. Researchers there are ambitious, connected and increasingly productive, and yet many still face barriers at every step of the journey, from winning funding to finding collaborators to getting published.

To understand what that looks like in practice, Elsevier, the Elsevier Foundation and Research4Life surveyed researchers across more than 73 countries, and heard from institutional leaders. Together, their voices show where the research system is working, where it isn’t, and what would make the biggest difference.

Building research capacity is just the starting point to make genuine progress toward full participation, authorship and leadership in global research. Dive into the findings and recommendations, and use them to start conversations in your own institution.

detail.abstract: Changes to AI-supported processes can each preserve timely human intervention when assessed separately while jointly exhausting a shared resource or exceeding an intervention mandate. This paper proposes linked conceptual representations for assessing such interdependent changes. The unit of analysis is a change set and its shared dependencies. Corrective reachability provides the assessment criterion: whether a specified corrective action remains feasible before a relevant process-state boundary. Two type-level views distinguish capabilities and information objects from actors, decision rights and accountability. A scenario view identifies shared actors and alternative configurations; a process model locates joint assessment before approval and checks its continued applicability before activation. A hypothetical banking example illustrates separate and joint assessments against the same initial configuration. A proposed study compares the linked representations with an equally informed process-and-role baseline, requiring both groups to assess individual and combined changes. The intended contribution is a purpose-specific modelling approach to identifying and explaining change interactions. Comparative diagnostic value remains to be demonstrated.

detail.abstract: Startup firms increasingly use crypto airdrops rather than conventional cash rebates to acquire early users and stimulate network effects. The two instruments differ in more than payment form. A cash rebate is normally tied to a verified purchase and requires an immediate cash outlay. An airdrop can reward observable platform activity, distribute a transferable token from a project treasury, and attract speculative participants who seek the reward without becoming genuine consumers. We study how these airdrop hunters change the strategic value of token-based customer acquisition. Our analysis identifies two opposing forces. Hunter activity creates subsidy leakage because reward value is allocated to nonconsumers, but it can also generate market exposure by increasing visible activity, discussion, and product discovery. The balance between these forces depends critically on network intensity and the startup's financing needs. When network effects are weak, hunter-generated exposure can make an airdrop more profitable than a cash rebate. When network effects are strong, leakage becomes more consequential and induces a defensive response in which the firm restrains both its token reward and product price. Airdrops can also reduce the first-period cash burden of customer acquisition, although deferral changes the timing rather than eliminates the economic cost of the reward. The findings distinguish the marketing value of speculative participation from the liquidity value of flexible reward timing and provide guidance for firms designing early-stage acquisition campaigns.

detail.abstract: Prediction markets rely on a resolution process that converts event outcomes into contractual payoffs. We study how experiencing a dispute over market resolution affects traders' subsequent trading activities on Polymarket. Using 814 matched pairs of disputed and undisputed events and a stacked difference-in-differences design, we find that dispute experience leads to a modest decline in weekly trading volume but a 1.43-percentage-point increase in realized returns on subsequent purchases. To understand these effects, we further investigate changes in traders' investment strategies on portfolio selection and investment timing. Following a dispute, traders shift their purchases away from markets with higher settlement risk toward those with lower risk. They also enter markets later, exit positions before resolution more often, and hold positions for a smaller fraction of the market lifecycle. Mediation analyses reveal that these adjustments have competing implications for investment performance. While shifting toward lower-risk markets and exiting positions earlier are positively associated with returns, delayed entry is negatively associated with returns. We further document heterogeneous responses across dispute types and trader characteristics. Together, our findings highlight how dispute experience reshapes trading strategies and investment performance, offering implications for the design and governance of prediction markets.

detail.abstract: We examine how patent protection shapes firms' voluntary disclosure incentives through its effect on financing. We hypothesize that weaker patent protection reduces the collateral value of patents, prompting firms to substitute secured debt with unsecured debt. Because unsecured creditors rely more heavily on information about firms' future cash flows, this shift increases disclosure incentives. Exploiting the 2014 U.S. Supreme Court Alice decision, which weakened protection for certain patents, we find that more Alice-exposed firms become more forthcoming during earnings conference calls. The disclosure response is stronger among firms facing debt-related financial constraints, firms that previously pledged patents as collateral, and firms with more redeployable patents. However, the response is attenuated among small firms and firms facing greater product market competition, consistent with heightened proprietary costs of disclosure. We also find that affected patents become less likely to be pledged as collateral and that exposed firms reduce their reliance on secured debt. Our findings identify a financing channel through which patent protection influences voluntary disclosure.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of changes in maintenance margin ratios on volatility, open interest, trading volume, and bid-ask spreads in one-month futures contracts. The maintenance margin ratio is defined as the required maintenance margin relative to contract size. While clearing houses use margin requirements to manage risk and maintain financial stability, anecdotal evidence suggests that higher margins may exacerbate market stress. Identifying these effects is difficult because margin requirements are adjusted in response to market conditions. To address this endogeneity, the paper exploits institutional features of clearing houses to construct an instrumental variable that identifies exogenous variation in maintenance margin ratios. Using data on one-month futures contracts across 15 assets, the analysis shows that a one-standarddeviation increase in the maintenance margin ratio reduces open interest by 6.13% and trading volume by 2.67%. Liquidity declines by 7.51%, while volatility of returns increases by 2.59%. A theoretical model explains the identification strategy and provides a rationale for the empirical findings.

detail.abstract: This study examines voluntary disclosure in a strategic setting where two competing firms decide whether to disclose private signals that are substitutes or complements. We show that equilibrium outcomes depend on information interactions. With moderate disclosure costs, substitute signals lead to an asymmetric equilibrium-one firm discloses while the other withholds because one firm's disclosure reduces the other's marginal value of disclosure. In contrast, complementary signals lead to a symmetric equilibrium-either both firms disclose or neither does-because joint disclosure generates more value than unilateral disclosure. These findings highlight information complementarity's role in shaping disclosure incentives, extending the literature that largely assumes substitutability.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an overlapping-generations model of a sandwich generation in which middle-aged households allocate scarce time and resources across market work, fertility, child quality, and support for elderly parents. The central distortion is that households overallocate time to elderly support due to strategic bequest motives. Households underinvest in child quantity and quality because distortionary payroll taxation makes caregiving time privately cheaper than its full social cost. Since human capital depends on both educational expenditure and parental time, optimal policy taxes intergenerational caregiving, provides a lower subsidy for childrearing time than for educational expenditure, and divides old-age social security between pension benefits and work-contingent labor subsidies. A calibrated illustration shows a welfare loss of about 7.8 percent relative to the efficient allocation, while the optimal fiscal response places greater weight on childrearing-time subsidies than on expanding pension transfers. More broadly, the analysis links population aging and low fertility through competition for scarce household time within families.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how views on climate change shape household inflation expectations. Us-ing a new representative survey of Dutch households, we elicit perceptions of climate change, the green transition and climate policies, and their expected effects on long-run inflation. House-holds expect climate change, the green transition and three types of climate policies – carbon pricing, support for the green transition and support for green innovation – to raise inflation and inflation volatility over the next ten years. Climate change is expected to have the largest effect, while support policies are expected to have the smallest. These results suggest that climate-related beliefs are linked to the anchoring of inflation expectations and that support policies for the green transition and green innovation may facilitate the net-zero transition while keeping in-flation expectations relatively well anchored. We also document significant heterogeneity across households. Expected inflationary effects of climate change are larger among respondents who anticipate more severe global warming and extreme weather. Climate-related inflation concerns are widespread across demographic groups.

detail.abstract: This article investigates whether a probabilistic intraday risk signal can be transformed into a dynamic exposure policy that reduces extreme losses after accounting for hysteresis, transaction costs, and execution constraints. Using S&P 500 (ES) and Nasdaq-100 (NQ) futures, the study evaluates a common policy that retains a previously established multiscale predictive model and reduces exposure to 25 % when the calibrated probability of an extreme event reaches 0.50. Full exposure is restored when that probability falls below 0.20, subject to a minimum holding period of 30 minutes in the reduced-risk state. The study distinguishes the historical results used during methodological development (2004-2023) from a subsequent economic evaluation conducted over a single continuous period from January 1, 2024, to November 2, 2026. This evaluation window comprises 734 trading sessions per market and uses a full-exposure benchmark equivalent to four micro futures contracts, under explicitly specified cost scenarios. Under the baseline cost scenario, the policy reduces daily downside semivariance by 26.26 % in ES and 68.71 % in NQ, while 95 % Expected Shortfall decreases by 17.37 % and 48.25 %, respectively. Nevertheless, cumulative net profit is substantially lower than that of the benchmark. The Sharpe ratio also declines in both markets. Maximum drawdown improves by 33.75 % in NQ but deteriorates by 2.53 % in ES. The reduction in downside risk persists under a scenario with higher execution costs. The results show that a hysteresis-based policy applied to risk probabilities can preserve meaningful protection against extreme losses, particularly in NQ, without necessarily improving profitability or risk-adjusted performance. The main contribution is to characterize empirically the distinction between the persistence of useful risk-control information and its ability to generate net economic value.

detail.abstract: This study examines how traffic congestion influences corporate cash-holding policies. We find that firms headquartered in more congested areas hold significantly higher cash reserves. This effect is stronger for firms with operations concentrated near their headquarters and for those in industries with high in-person requirements, but weaker for those located in states with greater transportation infrastructure investment. Using a formal mediation framework, we show that traffic congestion increases precautionary cash holdings by disrupting firms' outbound and inbound logistics, thereby increasing the uncertainty surrounding operating cash inflows and procurement costs. Further, we find that higher abnormal cash holdings mitigate the adverse effects of traffic congestion on future firm performance, are associated with greater subsequent capital expenditure, and are valued more highly by investors. Collectively, our findings highlight how firms adjust their liquidity policies to manage the persistent operational frictions created by traffic congestion.

detail.abstract: Geographic mobility can weaken reputational discipline by allowing financial advisors to escape consequences of misconduct. detail.abstract: Intellectual property (IP) plays an important role in promoting innovation, scientific advancement, creativity, industrial development and sustainable economic growth. In the contemporary knowledge-based economy, intellectual property rights (IPRs) provide legal mechanisms for recognising and protecting the outcomes of human intellectual activity, including inventions, products, processes, methods, artistic works, scientific contributions, cultural expressions and traditional knowledge. Their significance extends beyond commercial ownership to include technology transfer, entrepreneurship, agricultural development, public welfare, cultural preservation and environmental sustainability. The United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) provide an important framework for understanding the contribution of intellectual property to global development. This article examines the relationship between intellectual property and the SDGs, with particular reference to innovation in products, processes, methods, scientific research and social development. It analyses copyright and related rights, including economic rights, moral rights, performers' rights, broadcasting reproduction rights and producers' rights. It further examines industrial property, including patents, industrial designs, trademarks, geographical indications, protection of new plant varieties and semiconductor integrated-circuit layout-designs. Other important aspects, including traditional knowledge, traditional cultural expressions, folklore, trade secrets and protection against unfair competition in private and public services, are also considered. Drawing primarily upon Indian intellectual property legislation and relevant international agreements, including the TRIPS Agreement, the Paris Convention and WIPO instruments, this article argues that intellectual property should be understood as an instrument for inclusive and sustainable development. It concludes that an effective intellectual property framework must balance innovation incentives with public interest, equitable access, cultural preservation, technology transfer and fair benefit-sharing.

detail.abstract: Does government equity support insure investors against future losses or improve trading opportunities during stress? We study China's equity-market interventions using documented events, crisis-matched counterfactuals, trading, options, and exposure-sorted returns. Across 21 high-confidence clusters, six-day abnormal returns average 2.28%, with the price response concentrated in the first week. Trading value increases, but the large-trade net-selling share does not change significantly. For 16 clusters with option data, QVIX rises by 2.34 volatility points relative to matches, contrary to a simple downside-insurance prediction. In calm months, intervention exposure carries a negative industry-level premium (−0.61% per month), whereas January 2026 state divestment produces no detectable negative exposure-sorted return spread. An alternative official-announcement event list does not reproduce the turnover and QVIX results. The findings distinguish temporary price-and-liquidity support from credible downside protection, while neither identifying investors' liquidation motives nor establishing a causal government-purchase effect.

detail.abstract: Individual behavior can have several equilibria at the same reward. When choices also change market prices, which information is needed to determine whether a contract or productivity change raises a sector's stationary knowledge stock in every equilibrium? We extend behavioral-growth comparisons to interacting knowledge stocks and competitive task markets. Effort ranges alone are insufficient: other tasks supplied alongside effort change prices and can reverse the comparison. We derive a necessary-and-sufficient test when sectoral responses can be implemented together, the lowest target response exceeds its old stock below a reward threshold and falls short above it, and other sectors' maximum responses satisfy monotonicity and contraction conditions. In a personal-rule application, increasing workers' earnings shares raises knowledge under minimum-and maximum-effort allocations but lowers it under an intermediate-rule allocation. detail.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly treated as visual decision systems, yet the same wrong answer can come from different failures. The output may no longer separate two classes, or it may separate them and apply a displaced decision criterion, and a confusion matrix cannot tell these failures apart. In this study, we separate criterion bias from separability loss with signal detection theory and compare the output with a linear probe of the final hidden state. Label-free calibration references, cross-dataset transfer, layer-wise readouts, and two interventions further diagnose where each failure emerges. We use facial emotion recognition as a case study and test four open VLMs on six face datasets of posed, synthetic, and in-the-wild images. Every model places the fear/surprise criterion on the surprise side on every dataset. The error generalizes across models and datasets, but its failure mechanism does not. On posed and synthetic faces, the output still separates the two emotions, and the shifted criterion survives every label-free reference. On in-the-wild images, content-free calibration removes most of the shift for three models, and the output separates the two emotions less well. Anger and disgust fail in yet another way, since their distinction is decodable from the final hidden state but weakly reflected in the output on posed and synthetic faces. A correction fitted on one image type transfers poorly to the other, so the failure mechanism cannot be inferred from the confusion alone.

detail.abstract: To realize a sustainable society, Japan needs to achieve carbon neutrality (CN) by 2050 and implement further disaster prevention measures to deal with future natural disasters. Local governments are currently tackling these long-term challenges separately rather than through an integrated approach. To implement effective measures, however, a new approach that promotes interdisciplinary and integrated policies across government departments is required. In this study, we surveyed the employees of multiple local governments (municipalities) to investigate their views regarding the integration of CN and disaster prevention policies. The responses were analyzed to determine whether adopting the perspective of "Imaginary Future Generations" (a method proven to induce "futurability") can contribute effectively to promoting policy integration. The survey participants answered questions from the perspective of current generations before answering the same questions from the IFG perspective. A statistical analysis indicated that the application of the IFG perspective increased the tendency to accept burdens on the current generations, increase enthusiasm for interdepartmental collaboration, and strengthen the current generations' sense of responsibility for future generations. Further, the results indicates that the adoption of IFGs helps participants to perceive the compatibility between CN and disaster prevention. The study also found that the application of IFGs was effective regardless of the personal characteristics of the survey participants, specifically their level of empathy for others. This study suggests that IFGs may be a useful mechanism for promoting the integrated management of CN and disaster prevention policies.

detail.abstract: We develop a news-based measure of perceived financial stress for Canada using more than 900,000 business and economic news articles from 1977 to 2026. Using a data-driven keyword discovery algorithm, we construct an interpretable News-based Stress Index (NSI) that tracks major stress episodes and captures periods when concerns about financial risks intensify despite limited market disruption. Using linear and quantile-augmented VARs, we show that news shocks orthogonal to financial shocks primarily reduce unsecured consumer credit by shifting its entire distribution, whereas market-based financial shocks primarily worsen downside risks to both credit and real activity. This highlights perceived financial stress as a distinct transmission channel operating through household precautionary behavior.

detail.abstract: Adam Smith distinguished prosperity per person from the wealth of a nation. I measure the latter using Barro-Becker dynastic preferences, taking one founder per unit of territory as given. Each founder's welfare evaluates alternative demographic histories. National wealth is the value of a statistical life times the effective number of lives per unit of land, valued in goods rather than consumption equivalents. Among 87 countries, the United States ranks nineteenth in Wealth but forty-eighth in stock consumption-equivalent welfare; China's Wealth is 45 percent of the U.S. level, versus 14 percent per person. Since 1500, Wealth for a representative world aggregate rose about 173-fold, versus 3,714-fold under ABJK's consumption-equivalent measure.

detail.abstract: Continuously traded equity perpetuals can support venue-specific price formation and risk transfer while a trader's cash-equity alternatives are unavailable or costly. They are related conditional modules, not a unified general equilibrium. Current funding parameters generically reprice exposure without changing net positions under fixed continuation risk, preferences, costs and feasible capital. Stronger funding need not reduce absolute basis, and a stationary continuation need not attract prices dynamically. H2 separates off-hours price formation, information incorporation and cross-market leadership. The unchanged pre-reform baseline retains negative or mixed return forecasts, truncated books, 22 of 36 eligible primary opening-window spread cells and censored price-adjustment diagnostics. detail.abstract:
On 29 October 2026 about $6.36 billion was taken from Binance's hot wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in a first wave of about twenty minutes. The FBI attributes the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean unit. This paper asks who owes what when a sanctioned state robs a systemic exchange, and in particular who answers for the public loss once the users have been repaid and the funds that escaped have reached a state under sanctions. It examines three duty-holders in turn: the custodian, the stablecoin issuers whose tokens could be frozen, and the state that attributes, designates and forfeits.

The analysis combines U.S. sanctions law, the 2023 Binance resolutions and the GENIUS Act with on-chain evidence from a signed fund-flow case traced with SanctionFlow from the attacker's main Ethereum wallet forward from the first theft transaction; the case is public at sanctionflow.io/flows/binance-hack-stolen-funds-ethereum. The case shows that 700 million USDT left the attacker's main wallet within nine minutes, before any freeze: 325 million was sold for ether, 170 million moved through Uniswap swaps and an Aave deposit, and 205 million stopped and is reported frozen. 60 million USDT became Aave collateral for a 19,762 WETH loan less than three minutes before the wallet holding it was blacklisted. Circle's single freeze caught all 823 million USDC. Binance's compromised hot wallet was still sending funds to the attacker 43 minutes after Tether had blacklisted the receiving address. Three kinds of freeze (issuer, protocol, network) acted at three levels and none at the level of a position.

Three proposals follow: a failure-to-prevent standard for systemic custodians under which "we were hacked" is a defense that must be proved, as it already is for a bank under UCC Article 4A, and under which repaying users does not discharge what is owed to the public; a default hold for registered custodial wallets at the issuer layer, an interoperable freeze standard and a disclosed time-to-freeze; and a graded emergency signal with a safe harbor, a legal status within the GENIUS Act's lawful-order definition where existing authority supports it, and screening capacity treated as public infrastructure. The paper also proposes six measures (time-to-freeze, address exit ratio, route disposition, freeze coverage, attacker-controlled value, cost of escape) for the next incident. The case covers Ethereum only; the attribution is the FBI's and is disputed by North Korea; the paper asserts no finding that any party violated any law.

detail.abstract: We provide causal evidence that cash holdings shape retail investors' disposition effect. Identification comes from quasi-random variation in the intraday timing of cash arrival resulting from earlier mutual fund redemptions. Consistent with the two-layered mental accounting model of Dai, Qin, and Wang (2026, Journal of Finance), investors receiving the cash shock exhibit a significantly weaker disposition effect in their stock trading. The effect operates almost entirely through increased loss realization, with gain realization largely unchanged. It also extends to deep-loss positions: cash-rich investors sell deep losers outright, while cash-poor investors sell only after prices rebound. The effects persist among investors facing weak liquidity constraints and concentrate among those who actively monitor their portfolio budgets. Holding more cash also improves the performance of selling decisions. Cash gives investors the psychological room to admit mistakes and start afresh.

detail.abstract: Automated systems increasingly assess the regulatory compliance of other automated systems. Existing research on algorithmic auditing, explanation and organisational governance identifies substantial risks, yet it does not always isolate the institutional decision to rely upon an automated compliance assessment. This article argues that the legally salient event is often not the production of an algorithmic score but its promotion into an authoritative reason for action. It calls this process authority laundering, without claiming the expression or the underlying concern is unprecedented. Through doctrinal analysis of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and General Data Protection Regulation, together with a bounded reading of the Court of Justice's SCHUFA and Dun S Bradstreet Austria judgments, the article develops a reliance-sensitive accountability model. The model differentiates evidential assistance, evaluative recommendations and dispositive institutional reliance, and proposes proportionate safeguards tied to contestability, evidential provenance, reviewer independence and the consequences of error. It neither asserts a free-standing EU-law duty to audit every compliance tool nor extends GDPR Article 22 beyond its personal-data setting. Its contribution is an operational account of the transition from automated evidence to institutional authority, and a falsifiable research design for testing whether reliance-sensitive controls outperform ordinary compliance review.

detail.abstract: How do local governments set property taxes when the industry their economy rests on collapses? Raising rates as assessed values fall protects revenue, but it preserves the bill owners face when their incomes have fallen too. I test whether that adjustment survives, using the boll weevil's damage to Southern cotton yields between 1892 and 1922. On decadal census data for 1890 to 1930 I compare counties of diering pre-weevil cotton intensity within the same state and decade, separating the levy into the part a state set and the part counties set for themselves. Counties did not protect the levy they set. For a tenpercentage-point increase in cotton intensity the county-purpose levy falls by 0.206 log points against an assessed base falling by 0.126. The levy decline survives the 1890 characteristics and the tenancy shares, at 0.124 and 0.118, and county linear trends attenuate it to 0.071 without removing it. The rate counties set is negative in every within-state specication, at-0.080 without baseline controls and-0.068 with them, but it shrinks and loses signicance once the 1890 tenant shares enter, so the levy rather than the rate carries the argument. A state set one millage for every county, so the state margin could only follow the roll, and the state-by-decade eects remove it: it is the paper's benchmark, not a nding. Local governments let the property-tax levy fall with a damaged base rather than protecting it.

detail.abstract: Problem Statement: Buyers test artificial intelligence (AI) tools by having reviewers grade output, but reporting guidelines do not require measuring the reviewers' accuracy. We ask what this ignorance costs and who should remove it. Methodology: A buyer admits or rejects a tool with a pass/fail count test, holding both error risks to 10% for every reviewer whose catch and false-alarm rates lie in a stated range. We derive exact minimum tests, when none exists, and the grid-best one-time bank of known-answer notes for measuring reviewers. Results: For AI scribes judged at true-error boundaries of 10% and 30%, a test needs 25 notes with error-free review and at most 75 with any known reviewer catching 60-100% of errors with up to 5% false alarms, but 732 with a reviewer known only to lie in that range: over a range this wide, ignorance costs far more than inaccuracy. Measuring an assumed team (97% catch rate, 0.5% false alarms) with a 51-note bank cuts expected notes per product to 139, and with larger banks across 20 products to 65; at worst, 352 and 179. For rare harmful errors (2% versus 6%), no test exists once false alarms may exceed about 1.6%. Practical Implications: Guidelines should require measured reviewer accuracy. One measurement serves every matched product, so it belongs with whoever tests the most: pooled across Ontario's 20 approved scribes, it cuts 14,640 notes to about 1,300 for the assumed team, or 3,580 at worst.

detail.abstract: This paper estimates which groups of first-round voters account for the 6.66 million-vote change in Lula's margin between the two rounds of Brazil's 2026 presidential election. A constrained transition model is fitted within each electoral zone, assuming that voters with the same round 1 choice behaved alike within a zone. The model attributes most of the change to round 1 abstainers who voted in round 2 and to round 1 blank and null voters, in roughly equal parts. Minor-candidate voters split almost evenly, and the finalists' own voters added a net 1.07 million. These conclusions hold across specifications in direction, not in exact size. Bootstrap intervals do not achieve their nominal coverage in this setting. Simulations calibrated to fourteen features of the data, with vote choice, turnout and loyalty allowed to vary within zones, show that the variation the data reveal inflates the combined contribution of abstainers and blank and null voters by about half a million votes; allowing for it, they account for about three-quarters of the change rather than 83%. detail.abstract: Municipal Police departments are rarely examined as agencies that enforce animal welfare legislation, while their annual statistics often reduce the representation of animal protection work to the administrative fines imposed. This paper examines the Municipal Police of Ierapetra, Crete, during 2025, through a retrospective descriptive analysis of its complaints and case logbook, its annual operational report, and supplementary institutional statistics. Animalrelated cases reached 573 out of 1,350 recorded complaints and cases (42.4%), constituting the largest category of recorded workload, followed by sanitation (236) and road traffic (167). Violations involving animals accounted for 7.5% of the 1,220 administrative violations across all department jurisdictions and 24.7% of the total monetary value of confirmed fines. Regarding animals, 91 administrative violations were confirmed against 45 individuals (amounting to €57,600), while 18 criminal case files, three arrests, and 12 temporary animal removals were also recorded. Furthermore, the department reported 1,320 named owner inspections involving 1,600 owned dogs and cats, the collection of 256 puppies and kittens, 44 other animal rescues, and preventive assistance for approximately 200 sheep and goats during natural hazards. Together, these four categories total 2,100 animals subjected to actions of varying intensity, a figure that does not equate to 2,100 rescues. Drawing on the literature regarding the enforcement gap, street-level bureaucracy discretion, and police performance measurement, this article organizes Ierapetra's indicators into five dimensions of measurement: recorded workload, operational activity, law enforcement outcomes, reach of protective actions, and verified outcomes. The records provide almost no data for the final dimension. Because the data are aggregate, rely partly on departmental estimates, and are not linked on a case-by-case basis, they show what the department did, but they cannot answer whether animal welfare actually improved. Nevertheless, if only fines are counted, a large portion of this work remains invisible.

detail.abstract:
This paper builds a measure of how exposed a company is to biodiversity risk using only free and public data, and then puts two questions to it. The first is whether what a firm says about biodiversity in its 10-K filings matches what it physically does. The second is whether the stock market prices that exposure. The measure is built from the ground up at the level of individual facilities, so, unlike measures drawn from corporate text or from footprint accounting, it does not depend on anything a firm chooses to disclose about itself. It adds a threatened-species dimension to the protected-area proximity that recent work has used, and combines the two so that a site scores high only when both are present.

The measure combines two things about each facility: how much legally protected or ecologically significant habitat surrounds it, and how many threatened species have ranges that overlap it. We aggregate the facility scores to the firm using emissions as weights, so that a firm’s exposure reflects the sites where it actually operates at scale. Before using the measure in either test, we check that it captures something real. Both channels predict recorded Clean Water Act discharge violations at facilities across the country, an outcome they were never fitted to, with conservation pressure the more robust to controls; the measure ranks sites in a way that matches where a conservation regulator would expect risk to concentrate; and it is stable from year to year.

Two findings follow. Corporate biodiversity disclosure is largely decoupled from physical exposure: how much a firm writes about biodiversity in its 10-K filings is explained by its size, its sector, and the filing year, and hardly at all by its actual footprint. Separately, firm-level biodiversity exposure is not detectably priced in the cross-section of United States stock returns over 2022 to 2025; with only 57 firms in the pricing sample this is a bounded result rather than a clean zero, ruling out a large premium but not a small one.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how labor market outcomes have evolved across occupations as AI capabilities advanced from generative AI chatbots to reasoning models and AI agents. We construct an occupational AI exposure score that measures the share of each occupation's work that AI could perform at each capability stage, and link the change in exposure to the Current Population Survey from January 2023 through June 2026, using first-difference and fixed-effects designs at the occupation and individual level, with 2017 to 2022 as a placebo period. We find that occupations with larger increases in exposure show no change in employment or unemployment relative to occupations with comparable workforces. However, the composition of the workforce in these occupations changed. The number of workers under 30 decreased by about 8 percent per standard deviation of the change in exposure, and the decline is concentrated among workers without a college degree and builds gradually from 2023. It is not accompanied by higher unemployment among young workers who were already in these occupations, which suggests a decline in entry rather than an increase in exit. The decline is smaller when remote work is held fixed, but it remains. On the other hand, college graduates aged 30 to 49 gained full-time employment. Part-time work declined, weekly hours increased slightly, and the workforce in these occupations became older and more educated. In sum, the early effects of AI appear in the composition of the workforce rather than in the number of jobs.

detail.abstract: This article examines the structural configuration of agricultural trade between the Russian Federation and the ten member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) over the period 2015-2024. Drawing on disaggregated bilateral trade data across HS chapters 01-24 sourced from ASEANstats and ITC Trade Map, the study applies four complementary analytical measures: Shannon export entropy to quantify product diversification, the Bilateral Revealed Comparative Advantage (BRCA) index to assess bilateral specialisation, the Balassa Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) index to evaluate global competitiveness, and the Trade Intensity Index (TII) to gauge the depth of mutual trade engagement. The analysis reveals a persistent structural asymmetry: ASEAN maintains a broadly diversified agricultural export portfolio toward Russia (average entropy 1.94), while Russia's exports to ASEAN are concentrated in cereals, fish, and vegetable oils (average entropy 1.42). BRCA results confirm complementary rather than competitive specialisation across the majority of HS categories. The TII remained above unity throughout the entire decade and accelerated from 1.17 in 2020 to 1.32 in 2024, indicating that bilateral trade intensity is deepening beyond globally predicted benchmarks. The post-2022 acceleration coincides with Russia's geopolitical reorientation away from Western markets. The article argues that the relationship rests on durable agro-climatic complementarities and intensifying structural interdependence, while identifying SPS regulatory divergence, logistical distance, and export policy unpredictability as the three principal constraints on further expansion.

detail.abstract: We construct firm-level exposure to the 2018 and 2025 US tariffs through own imports, suppliers' imports, and foreign retaliation, and estimate their joint effects using quarterly financial statements. Exposure is widespread and travels down supply chains, reaching firms that import little themselves. In 2025, cost exposure reduced sales and cost of goods sold equally within three quarters, by about 1.2 percent for the average direct importer and 0.5 percent through suppliers. Firms at least partly passed tariffs on to prices and shrank production rather than cutting margins. Retaliation instead compressed gross margins. The 2018 effects are small.

detail.abstract: Zhang (2025) reports that FinBERT sentiment of GDELT news headlines, fed to an XGBoost classifier, predicts the next-day direction of EUR/USD, USD/JPY and 10-year U.S. Treasury futures with cost-adjusted out-of-sample Sharpe ratios of 5.87, 4.65 and 4.65 and daily win rates of 66-73%. I rebuild the pipeline from the paper's description, following its event filter, sentiment scoring, feature set, model classes, expanding-window validation and cost assumptions on the paper's three assets, with headline text taken from article URLs rather than scraped pages. In a pre-registered test, the XGBoost strategy earns Sharpe ratios of -0.43, -0.05, and -0.73, with win rates of 49-52%, and the best of the 18 asset × timing × model combinations has a Sharpe ratio of only 0.02. A variant that deliberately feeds the model the next day's news also earns nothing, so misaligned news timing cannot explain the reported performance; this rejects my own pre-registered hypothesis that it would. In a post hoc illustration, a one-row shift in the lagged-return feature produces Sharpe ratios of 15-18, and applying it to a random 39-48% of days, a share chosen to match the reported win rates, yields Sharpe ratios of the reported order. The reported results are therefore unlikely to come from news sentiment. The findings agree with an independent replication by Andrews (2026), which tested EUR/USD, and extend it to the paper's other two assets and to a direct test of the timing mechanism.

detail.abstract:
Experts hold divergent views on AI and its potential impact on the labor market. Generative AI has the potential to improve workforce productivity by automating tasks, accelerating them, or reducing the skills required to perform them. As is true with any transformative technological change, there will be winners and losers. For example, automated telephone switching displaced switchboard operators but created new technical jobs in telecommunications maintenance and network management.

The rate at which AI diffuses through an economy and the effects it has on a labor market depend on factors such as industry composition, incumbent workers' skills, and the degree to which a nation’s infrastructure supports the many technical requirements of AI deployment. Despite the technological frontier being pushed forward almost exclusively in the United States and China, Israel and Singapore have seen the greatest level of AI utilization per capita. This suggests that AI innovators are not necessarily located in labor markets most ready to deploy and use generative solutions. This report outlines a framework for describing occupations in the context of AI, discusses labor conditions for large-scale AI adoption, proposes mitigation strategies that governments might implement to protect disaffected workers, and poses a series of open research questions that may be valuable to industry leaders and policymakers.
