detail.abstract: For hedge fund research reviewers, this report examines checks for selective reporting when a registered study is closed. At Axio, the proposed use is review of research records before their conclusions enter an evaluation; no product integration or saving in review time has been measured. This report makes no claim of originality. A pre-registration helps a reader only if someone can later check that the reported study followed it. The author wrote a falsification test for one way of doing that check. A research record is kept in a fixed JSON format (registration, hash commitment, event log, closure), and seven mechanical rejection rules, R1 to R7, each target one selective-reporting defect taken from Arnott et al. (2019) and Harvey and Liu (2015). The comparison arm gives the same information, rendered as plain text, to a generalpurpose language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) with one fixed instruction. According to the retained local records, the test plan, its thresholds and its decision order were frozen with a local SHA-256 hash before any code, record or label existed; this chronology has no external timestamp. For each of two cohorts a separate model session generated 33 synthetic records, 12 valid and 21 with one injected defect, without seeing the rules, and labels were locked before either arm ran. In the first (in-sample) cohort the rules flagged 21 of 21 defective records and rejected 0 of 12 valid ones. The language model also flagged 21 of 21 but rejected 6 of 12 valid records, which disqualifies it under the plan. In the second (out-ofsample) cohort the rules again scored 21 of 21 with 0 of 12 rejected, and the language model scored 17 of 21 with 0 of 12. The gap of 4 is below the pre-registered margin of 5. The pre-registered verdict for both cohorts is therefore ”compared, threshold not met”, and the report makes no claim that the rules add detection. A reduced rule set (R1, R2 and R7 only) missed 12 of 21 defects in both cohorts and is refuted. No confidence intervals are reported, because the plan forbids them: the records are constructed counterexamples, not a sample from any population.

detail.abstract: This book offers a reflective and introspective approach to anthropic crises —those that originate in human decisions, systems and behaviour— grounded in the lived experience of those who undergo, manage and study them. It starts from a central premise: managing under uncertainty is not merely a technical challenge but, above all, an epistemic and perceptual one. On that basis, the book opens a series of exploratory “windows” inspired by major thinkers: the expulsion of the other (Han), the misunderstanding of circumstances (Ortega y Gasset), the liberating escape into magical realism (García Márquez), reflexive impotence (Fisher), human relationships and information networks (Harari), antifragility (Taleb), the painful assimilation of technological change (Winner) and systems thinking (Bertalanffy and Senge). These perspectives are set against the VUCA, TUNA and BANI frameworks, the biases that filter the perception of the exceptional, and the limits of knowledge —the unknown unknowns and the unknowable— and are illustrated through thirty-two international and Uruguayan crisis cases, from Chernobyl, Enron and Odebrecht to ANCAP, PLUNA and the Caja Profesional pension fund. Two cross-cutting axes give the work its unity: double-loop learning (Argyris and Schön), which requires revising the assumptions that guide action rather than merely correcting the action itself, and antifragility, understood as the capacity to improve through volatility, error and stress. The book closes with lessons, recommendations and a roadmap based on piecemeal social engineering (Popper) for the governance and management of crises, so that each crisis finds us more lucid, more humble and better prepared than the last.

detail.abstract: Why and how do origin states in the global South protect their female migrant domestic workers (FMDWs) despite the high cost of coercive interstate bargaining? Despite their centrality, International Relations (IR) scholars have overlooked how precarity surrounding FMDWs reconfigures origin states' foreign policy strategies toward global South host states. Our case study of the Philippines shows how an origin state performatively engages in gendered migration diplomacy towards Kuwait, Syria and the United Arab Emirates. We argue that origin states position themselves as FMDW's masculinist protectors, by employing coercion, quid pro quo and lobbying to downplay their jurisdictional limitations and failure to generate local jobs. Although their strategies can yield varying outcomes, origin states tend to effectively instrumentalize coercion to gain material and ideational concessions, depending on their political interests, leverage, and alternatives. Rather than being powerless, we contend that origin states employ gendered migration diplomacy to show their leverage and negotiating capacity, despite asymmetric power relations in South-South bargaining. Overall, the article advances empirical and theoretical debates on migration diplomacy, feminist IR and South-South labour migration by recentring origin states' gendered migration diplomacy as a bargaining instrument and a conceptual tool to examine gendered power politics international migration.

detail.abstract: We study how the linguistic complexity of financial advice affects trust in the advisor and the adoption of the advice. We posit two causal channels with opposing effects. Complexity increases the perceived competence of the advisor, which promotes trust and advice adoption, but it also decreases the perceived intelligibility of the advice, which has the opposite effect. We test this 'Complexity-Trust-Advice' model in two preregistered, incentivized experiments in which 1,435 participants with stock market experience made investment decisions on NYSEtraded stocks after receiving advice from a human or an algorithmic advisor. In both studies, the competence channel dominates, so that complexity has a positive indirect effect on trust and advice adoption, and complexity has no effect beyond these two channels. The same mechanism applies to algorithmic advice, but the competence gain generated by complexity is significantly smaller for an algorithm, whereas the intelligibility cost is unchanged. Algorithmic advice is not adopted more often than human advice.

detail.abstract: We develop a framework for implementing a desired portfolio path across temporal scales and strategic and tactical sleeves. Rather than decomposing the inputs to portfolio construction (returns, risks, or signals), the framework takes the target portfolio as given and applies a linear multiresolution decomposition to the position process itself, that is, to the portfolio weights. This decouples portfolio construction from implementation: any upstream method can supply the desired path, and the framework addresses only its downstream implementation. In the quadratic benchmark, the full-path implementation problem is solved exactly in the Fourier (spectral) domain. For a fully invested portfolio, a constant-preserving decomposition places the net budget in the slow component while finer detail components represent zero-budget reallocations. Quadratic trading costs impose the exact frequency penalty 4 sin 2 (ω/2), so optimal implementation of the desired holdings path acts as a low-pass filter. The zero-frequency mode carries the net budget and is held by the strategic sleeve; when the strategic and tactical sleeves differ in holding and adjustment costs, joint optimization determines both the implemented amplitude of each zero-budget temporal mode and its allocation across sleeves. Under an economically interpretable ordering of those costs, the model yields a closed-form crossover frequency quantifying where the dominant allocation changes from strategic at lower frequencies to tactical at higher frequencies, and a dyadic band structure maps that crossover back to the scale decomposition. A synthetic illustration shows the crossover and its mapping to scales. Because the decomposition is exact and linear, the same full-path representation also supports retrospective attribution of return, risk, and turnover across scales and sleeves. We also note the relation of the spectral benchmark to transient impact, nonlinear costs, portfolio constraints, and state-space feedback control.

detail.abstract: We find no robust evidence that sustainability information predicts stock returns. Machine learning on 22 environmental characteristics from four providers predicts neither returns nor their component orthogonal to 45 conventional firm characteristics. The same protocol recovers the known predictability of conventional characteristics, and the sustainability models' confidence intervals exclude Sharpe ratios above half of that benchmark. Replicating the green-minus-brown evidence of Pástor, Stambaugh, and Taylor (2022), we show that its significance as a return predictor hinges on sample period, universe, sort granularity, and prediction target. Across 132 models that vary variables, sample period, and prediction target, none survives multiple-testing corrections.

detail.abstract:
Across various areas of business and society, tasks and decisions traditionally undertaken by humans are increasingly being delegated to AI agents. This expansion of delegation raises the question of how to govern AI agents so that their behavior serves the objectives of those who delegate to them. Building on the conventional principal–agent problem and agency theory, this paper defines the principal–AI agent problem and presents a framework of “AI agency theory” that systematizes its underlying mechanisms, cost structure, and governance instruments.

The paper first reviews conflicts of interest, information asymmetry, agency costs, and governance through incentives, monitoring, and the allocation of authority in conventional theory. It then takes as its baseline analytical object an AI that follows externally supplied objectives and does not pursue private interests of its own. Even in this case, delegation can fail because the principal cannot adequately communicate objectives, constraints, and priorities, or sufficiently observe, evaluate, and control the AI's behavior. This paper calls the divergence between the principal's intentions and the AI's behavior arising from these constraints on delegation “AI agency slack.” It defines AI agency costs as the governance costs of preventing, detecting, and correcting such divergence, together with the residual loss that remains after these measures. The corresponding governance instruments include the design and updating of instructions, monitoring, the specification of the scope of delegation, and the allocation of authority to approve, modify, and stop actions.

The paper next considers a relationship in which shareholders are the principal and an AI agent acting as a manager is the agent. Through comparison with corporate governance premised on human managers, it examines the arrangements for oversight and control that might be considered when management is delegated to an AI agent.

The discussion then extends to four relationships: managers and AI agents acting as workers; politicians and AI agents acting as bureaucrats; clients and AI agents acting as professionals such as lawyers and physicians; and limited partner (LP) investors and AI fund managers. For each relationship, the paper anticipates how conventional agency problems may change when human agents are replaced by AI, and what delegation losses and governance challenges may arise. The paper contributes by clarifying which elements of conventional agency theory should be retained and which should be reformulated for delegation to AI, thereby providing an analytical foundation for AI agency theory to understand diverse delegation relationships in firms and beyond.

detail.abstract:
Objective: To test whether substitution (using chatbot advice instead of contacting a health professional) among health-chatbot users goes with poor access or with reliance markers.

Materials and Methods: Cross-sectional 2025 Canadian Digital Health Survey (11,311 online-panel respondents; about 6200 health-chatbot users). Weighted logistic models gave adjusted percentage-point differences (7 Holm-adjusted primary tests). Exploratory common-scale sizing followed all other results.

Results: Of users, 42% reported substitution. Adjusted differences: no regular provider vs family doctor/nurse practitioner −2.7 (90% CI −5.9 to 0.5); dissatisfied vs satisfied with timeliness 4.0 (95% CI 1.0–7.1) and proximity 6.2 (3.0–9.5); high vs not-high trust 34.4; top vs bottom eHealth-literacy third 14.6 (11.3–18.0); weekly triage use 5.1 (−0.1 to 10.3). Resetting no-provider and dissatisfied answers lowered predicted substitution 4% (1.7 points; 0.9–2.6; exploratory, descriptive); attachment ran opposite.

Discussion: Dissatisfaction associations were modest; the prespecified rule returned “Access matters” on proximity alone, whose interval included 5 points. Under the exploratory rule, excluding trust, measured access and self-rated confidence did not clearly separate; breadth and trust held most explained variation, describing who substitutes.

Conclusion: Having no regular provider showed no evidence of higher substitution. Dissatisfaction, trust and self-rated literacy went with more substitution, without establishing motives. Substituters reported more walk-in (10.4), emergency (7.9) and regular-provider contact (3.3; 1.2–5.4); displaced care is not shown. Evaluations should include high-trust, engaged users and measure completed professional contact.

detail.abstract: Contemporary political economy faces a theoretical rupture between micro-level individual behavior and macro-level institutional evolution. Traditional models often rely on the "rational agent" assumption or aggregate macroeconomic analysis, failing to capture the non-linear decay of institutional media and systemic risks. This paper proposes a dynamic theoretical framework of institutional space, unifying power and wealth as vector fields that share a fundamental dimension (person•time), and demonstrating their macroscopic relationship of curl mutual generation. To bridge the micro-macro gap, we construct a three-tier analytical architecture: at the micro-level, Markov chains are employed to describe the state transitions of agents; at the meso-level, deterministic Feynman diagrams are introduced to characterize the discrete propagation and path interference of institutional events (Zhizi/Institutional Bosons); and at the macro-level, field equations with time-varying coefficients describe the decay and evolution of institutional media. The study demonstrates that classical economic equations (such as diminishing marginal utility and supply-demand equilibrium) are steady-state special cases of this framework when medium parameters are held constant. This theory provides a rigorous mathematical-dynamic foundation for quantifying institutional collapse, policy transmission failure, and periodic reset (the Jubilee mechanism).

detail.abstract: This paper develops a calibrated decision framework for evaluating artificial-intelligence investment when inference prices fall rapidly, but enterprise spending, implementation costs, and outcome uncertainty rise. The analysis combines a historical and scenario-based token-price series, a macro capital-allocation module, a firm-level return-on-investment calculator, a scenario portfolio heuristic, a Bayesian real-options staging model, and a stylized dynamic growth model. The central result is not a point forecast. It is a governance proposition: declining token prices do not imply declining total cost of ownership, and the economic value of AI depends more on adoption volume, complementary organizational investment, realized productivity, and the ability to abandon weak projects than on application-programming-interface unit prices alone. Sensitivity analysis shows that firm-level returns change sign as hidden implementation costs rise, while six-year net present value is dominated by the productivity path. Immediate full-scale deployment has negative expected value across all modeled tiers under the assumed failure distribution, whereas staged pilots generate positive option value by limiting downside. Extending the staging model to imperfect pilot information shows that the staged strategy retains its advantage until the pilot's false-pass rate exceeds approximately 0.73, so the result is robust to substantial diagnostic noise rather than being an artifact of perfect-information assumptions. The macro model is highly sensitive to knowledge-spillover assumptions and should be interpreted as comparative statics rather than as an estimated structural forecast. The paper concludes that AI should be managed as a portfolio of real options subject to explicit hurdle rates, risk budgets, evidence standards, and stagegate rules.

detail.abstract: A price cap is a policy tool that cushions the spread of price shocks in an emergency and keeps economic activity going. It can be expected to help anchor inflation expectations, blunt the incentives for precautionary buying and hoarding, and make costs more predictable for firms and the public sector, while buying a critical window in which to secure alternative sources of supply and prepare fiscal measures. A comparison of major economies shows both direct price management and subsidy-based policies cushioning price increases. From March to August 2026, energy prices in South Korea, China, and Thailand rose an average of 15 percent year on year, 9.9 percentage points less than the 24.9 percent recorded in the United States and Germany, while in Japan, which stabilized prices through subsidies, they fell by an average of 4.5 percent. Korea's results have been relatively good, less because it eliminated price increases than because it kept them from widening further. From August to September, the year-on-year rise in Korea's gasoline prices held almost steady, moving from 11.8 to 11.9 percent, while the rates in Thailand, the United States, and Germany widened again over the same period. Exchange rates, taxes, and the lag before price changes pass through all play a part, however, so care is needed before reading the observed gaps between countries as the net effect of the price cap. Going forward, policy should combine temporary cushioning, targeted support, supply stability, and conditional normalization, rather than expand price ceilings across the board. That means adjusting the caps to reflect international prices and supply and demand conditions, settling losses transparently, targeting support at vulnerable groups and hard-hit industries, and diversifying supply and improving efficiency at the same time. The policy's performance should be judged not on price stability alone but on the full picture: the net burden on households, real output and exports in industry, supply stability, and the fiscal burden.

detail.abstract: The stability of banks is a key element of financial system resilience, while the management of banks' liquidity, credit and growth risks is at the heart of regulation. This paper explores, first, if there is a nonlinear relationship between liquidity risk, credit risk, loan growth, and bank stability, and, second, whether capital adequacy adds to or modifies these relationships. The study uses a sample of 30 commercial banks in Bangladesh in 2015-2024, employing a two-step System GMM methodology to account for the dynamic nature of stability and potential endogeneity. Liquidity risk and credit risk are both nonlinear on stability, with identifiable turning points, although formal validation of the curve shape is strongest for credit risk, and negatively affect stability in linear form; loan growth's effect on stability is also nonlinear, with an identifiable turning point. Although capital adequacy does not have any significant direct impact, it does significantly change the liquidity risk and loan growth effects on stability, but not the effect of credit risk. The results indicate that the impact of capital adequacy on stability is selective and not across the board, providing risk-specific insights for the regulation of banks in emerging markets.

detail.abstract: How many distinct exposures does a portfolio hold? Existing effective numbers answer adjacent questions instead: they count positions without regard to redundancy, or count variance-generating bets in a representation the analyst chooses. We introduce the effective number of distinct exposures (ENDE): one divided by the average squared correlation between two holdings, each weighted by its standalone risk. The contribution is the combination and the case for it: an argument for measuring quantity by standalone risk rather than capital, the recognition that breadth is relative to a partition the investor chooses, and evidence on real portfolios that the distinction changes conclusions. ENDE is one cell of a single construction with two parameters, and the only one of nine measures we compare that satisfies all seven properties a count of distinct exposures should have; the nearest competitor fails exactly one. On the US equity market read at thirty industries, ENDE is about two against a standalone-risk count of about seven.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how concentrated pricing power shapes the right to health. Article 43 of the Constitution promises the highest attainable standard of health. Kenyan patients meet that promise at a series of commercial gates. Patent holders, suppliers, pharmacies and insurers each stand guard. Each gate converts discretion into price. Verified data trace that conversion. Households still fund about a quarter of health spending out of pocket. A survey found median markups of 177 per cent locally. The public purchaser registers 32.2 million members. About five million pay premiums. That gap leaves the public scheme short of revenue. Two concepts organise the as purchaser. Does a dominant public buyer escape duties it imposes on firms? Four strong objections are met within the argument. Procurement reform without margin surveillance merely relocates the problem. Each proposal is evidence led. Each proposal regulates evidence and burdens, not prices. It concludes that enforcement and adjudication must form one channel. Otherwise the right remains a promise for those who can pay.

title: St. Augustine and the Synthesis of Natural Law: Navigating the Saeculum and Covenantal Statesmanship

detail.abstract: This paper examines St. Augustine of Hippo’s synthesis of Christian theology with the classical natural law tradition and its implications for Christian statesmanship. Augustine reformulated the impersonal cosmic reason of the Stoics by grounding the eternal law (lex aeterna) in the personal will and wisdom of a triune Creator, with the natural law (lex naturalis) as its imprint on the rational soul. Drawing on Chroust (1944), TeSelle (1988), Fogleman (2019), Nelson (2020), Alimi (2023), and Budziszewski (2011, 2023), the paper traces the maturation of Augustine’s view of temporal law from early rational optimism to a more regulatory and remedial account; the covenantal logic of Adam’s representation of humanity and its political consequences; and the doctrine of dual citizenship, in which Christians live as pilgrims in the saeculum while seeking the peace of the earthly city. It reviews the debate among Markus, Milbank, and Mathewes over whether the saeculum is a neutral space, and it develops an account of Augustinian statesmanship as service rather than domination, governed by the distinction between use and enjoyment (uti and frui). The paper concludes that Augustine’s architecture of ordered love supplies a durable moral and procedural scaffolding for justice and stability in a fallen world.

detail.abstract: Founders and their backers often treat the timing of an initial public offering (IPO) as a strategic choice, yet the new venture literature has paid less attention to how market conditions at listing shape post-IPO performance than to the pre-IPO attributes of firms. We develop four propositions on how the IPO window, media sentiment at listing, and signal quality jointly shape whether early listing benefits persist, and we consider how artificial intelligence tools may alter the information environment in which timing decisions are made. We test the analysis plan on a sample of 500 European IPO firms. The results show that the analysis recovers the window, sentiment, and signal effects with high detection rates, and that the inverted-U shape of sentiment is recovered with a turning point near its true value. The paper contributes to entrepreneurial finance research on market windows and to the study of how new information actors affect listing outcomes.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we seek to answer the following research question: What effect do consumption outcomes have on monetary policy? We argue that consumption outcomes, measured through the PCE (personal consumption expenditures) price index and the growth of consumer spending have largely become the primary input into the policy decisions made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), and this is a departure from what the Framers intended with respect to the monetary provisions set forth in the Constitution. The Framers treated money as what some might call a measure, placed next to weights and measures in Article I, and gave Congress (notably not an independent committee) the power to regulate value. Through amendment to the Federal Reserve Act, the interpretation in the Legal Tender Cases and the Gold Clause Cases respectively, and the committee adopted frameworks that serve as what Frohnen and Carey (2016) refer to as quasi-law, one can observe that monetary policy has shifted from keeping the measure honest toward managing consumer demand. Analyzing Higgs (2012) and Strang (2019), we identify eight differentiations between current policy and original intent and we propose a statesmanlike response that highlights congressional accountability while still not abandoning the stability gains in the modern (nationalized) economy.

detail.abstract: The risks artificial intelligence creates for social protection extend beyond unemployment counts. Even as aggregate income grows, wage-linked pension contributions may contract if growth accrues disproportionately to capital, labor's income share falls, and contribution coverage fails to offset that decline. Focusing on K-shaped divergence, this article connects task reorganization in highly educated occupations, young workers' opportunities to enter professional careers, changes in the evaluation of cultural production, and population aging within a single institutional transmission chain. The resulting dual crisis involves pressures on workers' current incomes and continuity of protection alongside pressures on the long-term financing of pension systems. Drawing on task-based theories of technological change, workplace studies of generative AI, experiments on the evaluation of art, and China's pension insurance accounts, the article develops a minimal model of income distribution and fund cash flow. It establishes the necessary and sufficient condition under which aggregate income growth and declining contribution revenue coexist. It further proposes testable links among narrowing occupational entry routes, interrupted accumulation of entitlements, and the limited transmission of growth gains into social protection financing. Whether AI-generated gains support pension provision depends on the distribution of returns, the income sources covered, and public financing rules. Improvements in model capability alone cannot accomplish this conversion. The severe scenarios examined here serve as conditional institutional stress analyses.

title: Beyond Fixed Genders: Wartime Sexual Violence, Asymmetric Victimhood, and Institutional Invisibilities

detail.abstract: This paper argues that wartime sexual violence is not a performance of fixed binary genders but a "gendering act" that masculinizes perpetrators and feminizes victims, regardless of biological sex. Examining conflict-related sexual violence across three analytical axes-the legal reduction of male sexual abuse to non-gendered torture, distinct bodily and reproductive harms such as forced castration versus forced impregnation, and gendered post-conflict stigma-this study demonstrates how patriarchal hierarchies shape institutional, clinical, and media responses. By highlighting these structural blind spots, the paper reveals how institutional and domestic legal shortcomings perpetuate gendered victimhood and ultimately argues for comprehensive, survivor-centered policy frameworks that account for the diverse realities of all conflict survivors.

title: From Categorical Probability to Geometry from Histories Stochastic Path Systems, Predictive Quotients, and Operational Reconstruction

detail.abstract: Voevodsky's categorical probability describes a stochastic process through kernels and interval-indexed systems of paths, in which the object followed through time may carry structure that its pointwise observations never record. His unfinished Singletons poses the matching inverse problem for a branching population: the surviving genealogy is observed, and the mortality that shaped it is not. Geometry from Histories starts from the other end. It takes the observed history as primitive, identifies two histories when every admissible future test gives them the same law, and reads a metric from the resulting quotient. The two constructions meet at a single place, the descent of extension kernels through the quotient map. When extension is constant on the fibres of the quotient, the composition law of the path system survives reconstruction. When it is not, the proposed state has discarded information that its own evolution requires. The manuscript states this criterion, separates it from the stronger realization theorem of Zhorin [4, 5], and distinguishes identifiability, a property of the map from mechanisms to observable laws, from predictive sufficiency, a property of the map from histories to future laws. Neither quotient determines the other. Finite-state, genealogical, and clinical event-history examples follow. The extension to general interval-indexed path systems remains a research problem.

detail.abstract: An et al. (2024) report a stronger disposition effect in loss portfolios and attribute it to portfolio-level mental accounting. We show that measuring performance from current holdings can generate this finding. Realized gains drop out, while retained losses remain, concentrating disposition-prone investors in loss portfolios. In matched samples, loss-portfolio investors' prior disposition effects are at least six times those of gain-portfolio investors. A model formalizes this sorting; simulations reproduce nearly two-thirds of the reported stock-portfolio gain interaction without portfolio-dependent selling. In experiments, including realized outcomes yields a precisely estimated zero interaction. These findings undermine the portfolio-level mental accounting explanation.

detail.abstract: Openness is a central but contested category in global artificial intelligence (AI) governance, yet policy debates often treat it as a binary property of developers, or even of states. This article asks how leading foundation model developers practice openness through release and licensing decisions, and what this implies for how openness is governed globally. We analyze an original longitudinal dataset of 1,313 model releases by twelve developers in the United States (US), China, France and Canada between January 2023 and October 2026. We find that openness is a property of model portfolios rather than of developers. We distinguish four configurations, defined by whether, and on what terms, a developer releases its most capable model: permissive, conditional, or non-commercial open flagship, or closed flagship with permissively licensed secondary models. Secondary models have converged on generic permissive licenses, while open flagships have moved towards bespoke conditions that target revenue rather than users. The sharpest division concerns whether third parties can inspect a developer's most capable model without permission: all US developers now withhold this, while developers elsewhere, except Baidu, allow it. Drawing on the notion of a "polysemous compromise" and on practice-based accounts of norm formation, we argue that the meaning of openness is being settled not by states but in license files, largely outside the public eye.

title: A Policy Framework for Regulating Excessive Television and Smartphone Use towards a New Social and Cultural Renaissance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of television broadcasting, smartphones, and mobile internet connectivity has transformed contemporary human life. These technologies have created unprecedented opportunities for communication, education, information access, entertainment, and public services. However, their excessive and increasingly pervasive use raises important questions concerning the allocation of human time, the quality of family relationships, independent thinking, educational practices, sleep, cultural participation, and community life. This article proposes a public-interest policy framework for regulating excessive television consumption and smartphone-based digital engagement without rejecting technological advancement. It argues that technology should remain an instrument serving human development rather than becoming a dominant force that determines everyday life. The proposed framework has two principal components: a structured national television broadcasting schedule and a differentiated approach to mobile communication and internet access based on legitimate human needs. The article further examines the distinction between essential needs, useful conveniences, and non-essential luxuries in the context of digital consumption. It proposes strengthening reading habits, independent learning, handwritten academic work, institutional digital education, family interaction, public intellectual forums, traditional theatre, street performances, and endangered cultural practices. It also recognises the technical, regulatory, constitutional, and practical limitations of controlling internet speeds through conventional network-generation classifications. Adopting a conceptual and policy-analysis approach, the article develops a framework for reclaiming human time and restoring balance between technological progress and social wellbeing. It concludes that a new social and cultural renaissance may become possible when technological systems are designed and regulated around human priorities.

title: Minister of God: Natural Law and Christian Kingship in the Thought of Thomas Aquinas

detail.abstract: This paper examines the architecture of Christian kingship in the thought of Thomas Aquinas as the culmination of the natural law tradition that preceded it. It traces the genealogy of natural law from the Stoics and Cicero, through Augustine’s two cities, to Aquinas’s integration of Stoic cosmic reason and Augustinian providence with Aristotelian political naturalism, in which the state is a natural institution ordered to the common good rather than merely a remedy for sin. The paper sets out Aquinas’s four tiers of law (eternal, natural, human, and divine), which keep kingly authority under higher measures, and his account of justice in its commutative, distributive, and legal forms as the defining excellence of the royal office. Drawing on McCormick (2018), Seipel (2015), Zuckert (2007), and Cendejas Bueno (2017), it considers the derivation of natural goods, the king as minister of God and keeper of a covenant, the subordination of the regnum to the sacerdotium, and Aquinas’s realism about the fomes of sin and the danger of tyranny. The paper concludes that the Thomistic synthesis offers a framework in which the political community participates in the divine plan, and in which the ruler is both ennobled and limited by a hierarchy of laws.

detail.abstract: Autonomous AI agents that discover, negotiate and pay on behalf of consumers force a foundational choice about the infrastructure beneath them: should agent identity, payment and accountability run on decentralized protocols (decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, stablecoin settlement, smart contract constraints) or on extensions of centralized platforms, card networks and API governance? This paper analyzes that choice through three legal lenses. In competition law, centralized architectures create layered gatekeeping positions across identity and payment authorization that self-preferencing rules were not designed to reach, while transparent on-chain state may facilitate tacit algorithmic coordination. In consumer protection, the absence of a consumer-side agent framework leaves platform-aligned agents free to serve merchant or platform interests, and leaves liability for agent error unallocated. In privacy law, centralized authentication requires data sharing with intermediaries, public ledgers create permanent and potentially de-anonymizable records, and institution-side foundation models erode the informational basis of consent. Drawing on the UK CMA’s 2026 agentic AI guidance, MiCA, the GENIUS Act, the Consumer-Driven Banking Act and Canada’s Stablecoin Act, the paper proposes a hybrid framework: decentralized identity for agent portability, rail-agnostic settlement, and on-chain authorization constraints with off-chain privacy. Market convergence suggests the architecture will be hybrid. The open question is whether its governance prioritizes consumer agency.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the first-year effects of Rx Kids, a citywide unconditional cash transfer program for pregnant women and infants in Flint, Michigan, on birth outcomes. Using city-level data on Michigan's largest cities from 2019 to 2024, I compare differencein-differences, synthetic control, and synthetic difference-indifferences estimators. I find little robust evidence that Rx Kids reduced low birthweight or preterm birth, or improved other core birth outcomes. Reported smoking during pregnancy declines consistently across specifications, but the estimate does not survive correction for multiple hypothesis testing, and because smoking is self-reported, the decline may reflect changes in reporting rather than a true reduction in smoking.

detail.abstract: The interdisciplinary field of intelligent computing combines computer science, mathematics, cognitive science and engineering to develop computational systems that can learn, reason, adapt and make intelligent decisions. Artificial intelligence, machine learning, neural networks, fuzzy logic, evolutionary computing and mathematical optimization are the cornerstones of intelligent computing. The fundamental frameworks for comprehending how intelligent systems learn, analyze information, resolve challenging issues and react to changing surroundings are provided by these theoretical stances. This chapter reviews the underlying concepts and theoretical foundations of intelligent computing, covering conceptual foundations, historical background and the important computational paradigms. Focuses on the use of artificial neural networks, probabilistic models, fuzzy inference, statistical learning, symbolic reasoning and optimization techniques inspired by nature to design intelligent systems. Furthermore, it explores the challenges of dealing with nonlinear behavior, ambiguity, lack of information, complex search spaces and adaptive decision making. The chapter also highlights the complimentary relationships between the different paradigms, as well as the evolution of hybrid intelligent systems, integrating many paradigms to improve computing efficiency, adaptability and reliability. The chapter discusses theoretical background and relevance of computational intelligence to recent research and technological advancements. It covers the mathematical and computing principles underpinning intelligent problem solving and explores their application to manufacturing, robotics, healthcare, education, finance and data analytics. The disadvantages of existing models, including computation, interpretation, dependence on data, scalability and generalization are paid particular attention. The chapter also discusses the philosophical and ethical ramifications of intelligent systems, with a focus on responsible AI development, responsibility, transparency, justice and privacy. Finally, it points to areas of novel research, including explainable AI, neurosymbolic computing, adaptive learning, quantum-inspired intelligence and the collaboration between humans and AI. Providing a systematic mapping of the theoretical concepts and computational techniques, this chapter provides a solid foundation for understanding Intelligent Computing and its emerging significance in scientific research, technological advances and intelligent decision-making.

detail.abstract: Spillovers pose fundamental challenges for causal inference as treatment assigned to one unit may affect the outcome of others, violating the no-interference assumption. Existing approaches, based on partial interference, exposure mapping, spatial, network, or structural frameworks, typically rely on strong assumptions about interaction structures and/or require uncontaminated control units to estimate relevant causal parameters. We revisit this identification challenge within the potential outcomes framework and provide the first formal analysis of how forecast-based counterfactual methods (FBCMs) can identify and estimate average treatment and spillover effects. Through simulations and an empirical application, we illustrate the main advantages and limitations of this new approach compared to the most widely used control-based counterfactual methods. We show that FBCMs can identify key aggregate causal effects even when spillovers are pervasive or the exposure mapping is unknown.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we study optimal reinsurance design under ΛVaR with risk aversion, where the function Λ is increasing. Under the expectation premium and the incentive compatibility condition on the ceded loss functions, we derive closed-form expressions for the optimal reinsurance treaties by minimizing the ΛVaR of the insurer's total risk exposure. We consider two typical classes of Λ. When Λ is a step function, a layer reinsurance treaty is shown to be optimal. Particularly, in the case of two-step function, we provide explicit expressions of the optimal reinsurance treaties. When Λ is continuous and strictly increasing, we find that the derived optimal reinsurance treaty is not necessarily piecewise linear. Comparisons with existing results and numerical examples are also provided to illustrate the proposed model and main results.

detail.abstract: Weekly energy prices provide timely information about monthly inflation, but their usefulness need not depend on estimating a separate coefficient for each week. We assess the value of this flexibility for United States Consumer Price Index (CPI) energy inflation using weekly West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude-oil and retail gasoline prices over 2005-2026. Matched comparisons hold the weekly observations, autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) errors, estimation window, and target history fixed. A separate applied comparison evaluates monthly-average regressors that use every available endpoint. Free coefficients on target-month WTI changes give no reliable accuracy gain over their block mean, although moderate gains remain unresolved. Monthly-average retail gasoline reduces nowcast root mean squared error by 43-60% relative to the ARMA benchmark in the main windows and schemes; adding WTI gives no reliable gain. Free gasoline coefficients improve on matched block means by 14.8% in contemporaneous comparisons but perform worse than the monthly-average regressor. With predictors lagged one month, the matched gain is an imprecise 2.7%; the larger 16.7% gain against the monthly average also changes endpoint coverage. Thus the predictor and the comparison benchmark both matter when assessing weekly flexibility. The retrospective evidence supports monthly averaging as a parsimonious benchmark, with prospective and historical release-time validation still needed.

title: The End of Software Copyright
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: The End of Software Copyright

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract:
The vast majority of coders and software companies today use AI-generated code or employ programmers who do; surveys suggest that nearly 90% of coders are using AI tools like Claude Code or Codex to write their software.

That code is uncopyrightable regardless of how it is made. There are three possibilities: 
First, the AI tool may replicate someone else’s proprietary code from its training data set. And if portions of their code are infringing, the law denies the user copyright protection even for the parts that are original that are intermingled with the infringing code.
Second, the AI tool may replicate open source code from its training data set. The viral nature of most open source licenses means that the user who incorporates that code, even unwittingly, has agreed to open their code in turn to copying by others.
Third, the AI tool may generate its own code. But AI-generated code is uncopyrightable.

In none of those cases is software copyrightable. The end of software copyright is nigh. Indeed, it may be here already. That doesn’t mean the end of the software industry, and probably not even the end of proprietary software. The industry may muddle through, and it may persuade Congress to change the law. But whatever future comes, the law of copyright and the software industry it underlies will never be the same.

detail.abstract: Many countries have explored or adopted carbon pricing--often in the form of emissions trading systems (ETSs)--to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Increasingly, many jurisdictions are considering intensity-based and product-level design elements to address practical issues of affordability, industrial competitiveness, and coverage of harder-to-abate sectors. Product-level, intensity-based tradable performance standards (carbon intensity standards) have been examined previously, but often in the context of a single sector or product, such as road transportation fuels. Here we apply such standards to major energy and energy-intensive products in a numerical capacity expansion model of the US energy system and compare results to mass-based policy alternatives, namely a carbon price and an emissions cap. At comparable realized carbon prices, lower commodity prices under the intensity approach reduce the extent of demand-side fuel and technology substitution, but most abatement from economy-wide pricing is still realized. For the same realized emissions, the mass-based policy results in modestly lower total costs, whereas the intensity approach results in substantially lower costs to consumers unless carbon revenues from the mass-based policy are nearly fully returned. We conclude by providing actionable insights related to the design of market-based emissions reduction policies and suggest several areas for future research.

detail.abstract: Policymakers widely view geopolitical risk as a supply shock. Using transaction-level data on U.S. imports, we show that it raises prices and lowers quantities along exposed sourcing relationships. Yet more exposed firms manage to reduce their average import prices and to import more. This reflects changes in sourcing composition, mainly the entry of new products through existing countries and suppliers. Firms' reaction is stronger when shocks are larger. Firms also adjust in response to geopolitical threats before disruptions occur. These results suggest that uncertainty about access to inputs leads firms to pay the fixed costs of reoptimizing their sourcing.

detail.abstract: More favorable consumption outcomes can make carry trades more vulnerable to funding disruptions by supporting larger positions in advance. I develop a currency-market model in which speculators absorb commercial hedging demand subject to funding constraints. Hedging demand and funding capacity jointly determine the price when the constraint binds; anticipated constraints transmit this valuation to earlier states without an imposed terminal exchange rate or frictionless benchmark. In an analytical equilibrium with slack capacity before stress and at entry, a greater pricing weight on adverse consumption states lowers both positions, with a larger reduction before stress that reduces the unwind and proportional depreciation. The physical funding process and carry incentive remain fixed. In a numerical economy with recursive preferences, gradual capacity reconstruction can delay the recovery of positions and currency values after normal consumption growth resumes. In contrast, financing can reopen, while weak consumption and the risk of renewed freezes continue to restrain exposure.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author competed as an entrant in the tournament studied, the Susquehanna Predictions Cup. The author is not affiliated with the contest's sponsor, its platform operator, Kalshi or Polymarket, and none of them sponsored or reviewed this paper.

detail.abstract: We recorded a play-money prediction-market tournament on the 2026 US midterms alongside Kalshi and Polymarket, which listed the same races. The play-money prices were compressed toward one half relative to Kalshi, with a logit slope between 0.71 and 0.87 over three weeks. For an entrant ten times behind who plays only for first place, when no bet has positive expected profit and the field is independent of one's bets, the chance of finishing first is at most 3.9%, the fair-casino bound of Dubins and Savage with a random target, and compression and thin order books cut the obvious longshot route to 0.3%. A strategy that buys stale play-money quotes once real money has priced a race call, and reinvests the proceeds, won 1.8% of simulated nights at mid-October book depth, averaged over two settlement rules, and 1.0% once its longshots win only as often as the simulator's own probabilities say; at the thinnest depth simulated, still five times deeper than election night's books, no planner won more than 1 night in 16,384. On the night, Kalshi's price for the winner reached 0.97 before the Associated Press call in all 31 contested races, a median 108 minutes earlier, and the play-money discount on called winners lasted hours, so the snipe was limited by capital, not speed. The entry finished at 97,486 of its 100,000.

detail.abstract: Using individual political campaign contributions to measure CEO and employee partisanship, I find that greater CEO–employee political distance is associated with less frequent management earnings forecasts, more reported material weaknesses in internal controls, and a higher likelihood of restatement. The forecast associations strengthen with longer CEO contribution histories and in firms with larger workforces, greater geographic dispersion, more business segments, and higher labor intensity. These patterns are consistent with political frictions in sharing information between employees and management. Supporting the measures' validity, CEO and employee partisanship predict whether CEOs sign public political statements and open letters, with politically distant CEOs being significantly less likely to sign on. Political distance between the CEO and employees is thus associated with lower voluntary disclosure provision and mandatory reporting quality.

title: Must Accurate Automated Home Valuations Be Hard to Explain? Evidence from Cook County

detail.abstract: In automated house valuation models, accuracy and transparency are desirable, yet they are often thought of as incompatible. Cook County's Assessor replaced township-level linear regressions with a LightGBM gradient boosting model, a leading machine learning valuation approach chosen for its accuracy although harder to explain. We show that no such trade-off may be needed by comparing a a recently developed transparent Bayesian hedonic model against the Assessor's own model, rebuilt or run from its public code and data. In suburban assessments at 1 January 2022 and 2023 and in predictions of 38,177 later sales across all 38 townships, the hedonic model's unadjusted values are more accurate, mainly because their overall level is closer to sale prices, and the model remains as accurate after both models are rescaled to the median ratio of value to sale price. It is also less regressive in two of three comparisons. Unlike the machine learning model, our model provides a predictive interval for each sale price. Measuring by the percentage of house prices within the 80% modelled interval shows that letting the model's error scale depend on the neighbourhood's price level improves calibration from 69% to 77% among the lowest-priced fifth of homes. Transparency costs no accuracy, and the model shows where its values are least certain: among lower-priced homes, where the fairness of assessment is most at stake.

detail.abstract: To address climate change, achieving carbon neutrality (CN) by 2050 and implementing disaster prevention measures to mitigate the risks of natural disasters associated with future climate change have become urgent challenges for humanity. To tackle these issues, new methodologies need to be explored for approaching them with an integrated perspective through collaboration between municipalities, taking account of effectiveness and long-term implications. In this study, we verified the effectiveness of developing integrated policy proposals using Imaginary Future Generations (IFGs), a proven method for generating "futurability" of people and society. Specifically, we incorporated the method of IFGs in a deliberative practice involving employees of multiple municipalities and officials of government agencies to explore integrated policies to address CN and disaster prevention. We then analyzed the discussions, decision-making, and responses to questionnaires. The results of the discussions and questionnaire responses by the discussion participants suggest that the adoption of IFGs is effective for generating different policy proposals (compared to current initiatives) and promoting cross-sectoral discussions that encompass the spheres of both CN and disaster prevention policy. Questionnaire responses also suggest that the adoption of IFGs reduces the perceived importance of factors such as "feasibility of policies" and "obtaining the understanding of residents and assembly," two key criteria for policy formulation, which can also be constraints when considering fundamental policy-making. The present study suggests that adoption of IFGs can promote policy proposals and decision-making in efforts to further the integration of policies relating to CN overcoming current constraints, thereby verifying the value of IFGs in generating "futurability."

detail.abstract: I develop a methodology for extracting narratives-endogenously-emerging interpretational patterns-from unstructured text. I define "narrative cacophony" as the presence of many salient narratives with contradictory pricing implications. Applying the methodology to 21,771 news articles from the 2025 tariff "Liberation Day" episode, I study how cacophony mediates the incorporation of public information. I document that cacophony dampens trade volume. Moreover, when there is less trade because of cacophony, narratives explain a smaller share of variation in daily returns. The incorporation of narrative information also slows and a delayed pricing-in effect obtains. Because markets incorporate information into prices through agents' trades in the face of disagreement, these findings suggest that information that is difficult to interpret (as captured by cacophonous narratives) is less well-incorporated by markets as agents are more reluctant to trade. * This paper could not have been written without the unwavering support of Jean-Edouard Colliard and Itzhak Gilboa. detail.abstract: Persistent crosscountry differences in long-run interest rates command a currency risk premium beyond the carry trade. Motivated by the Fisher equation, we estimate each country's long-run nominal rate in real time as the fair value of its 10-year yield given inflation and growth, and sort currencies on its differential to build carry *. Carry * earns 3.52% a year, with a higher Sharpe ratio than traditional and static carry, a significant alpha over both and over other currency factors, and a significant price of risk in the cross-section. Unlike carry, whose return is mostly static, two thirds of its return comes from updating positions as long-run rates move, and exchange rates do not offset the long-run part of interest differentials. The premium comes from the inflation part of the long-run rate, while the real part is not priced. Carry * loses less than carry in bad times but is more exposed to option-implied crash risk and oil risk.

detail.abstract: Bank markups have risen substantially, dispersion across banks has increased, and large banks now charge higher markups than smaller institutions. We develop a general equilibrium model in which persistent borrower and depositor relationships endogenously generate heterogeneous bank market power. Banks are dynamic two-sided intermediaries that compete for customers while inheriting partially captive borrower and depositor bases. Relationship capital creates a trade-off between current margins and future franchise value, generating endogenous loan markups and deposit markdowns that vary across banks. Regulatory constraints and costly external equity make market power on one side of the balance sheet affect pricing on the other, linking deposit markdowns and loan markups. Quantitatively, two-sided bank market power has sizable macroeconomic implications, reducing financial intermediation and lowering aggregate output. A permanent increase in the safe rate alters franchise values, leading banks with different customer bases to adjust loan and deposit rates differently.

detail.abstract: The effectiveness of the management of the Regional Budget (Anggaran Pendapatan dan Belanja Daerah, APBD) has generally been judged by how much of the budget is absorbed, even though high absorption does not necessarily improve the condition of the poor. This study analyzes the effectiveness of regional expenditure and social assistance expenditure in the Bekasi City APBD for 2023-2025 and describes how they relate to changes in the poverty rate. The study uses a descriptive quantitative approach with secondary data from the Budget Realization Report (Laporan Realisasi Anggaran, LRA) of the Bekasi City Government and data from Statistics Indonesia (BPS). Effectiveness is calculated as the ratio of actual realization to budget and then categorized according to Minister of Home Affairs Decree No. 690.900.327 of 1996. The results show that regional expenditure is fairly effective, with an average of 86.71%, but it declined from 88.83% (2023) to 85.92% (2024) and 85.39% (2025) because the budget ceiling grew faster than actual realization. Social assistance expenditure is effective, with an average of 98.01%. Over the same period, the percentage of the population living in poverty fell from 4.10% to 4.01% and 3.96%, with the pace of decline slowing from 0.09 points to 0.05 points. The effectiveness of social assistance and the decline in poverty moved in opposite directions, so high budget absorption does not guarantee that assistance reaches the right recipients. The link between the two can only be described descriptively, not as a cause-and-effect relationship. The Bekasi City Government is advised to set more realistic budget ceilings, use up-to-date poverty data such as DTSEN, and assess the success of spending by its impact on poverty reduction.

detail.abstract: Sylvamo Corporation (SLVM) is a global leader in the production of uncoated free-sheet (UFS) paper. Known as the “World’s Paper Company,” Sylvamo also has mills for production, including five outside of North America and two within North America. This diversification has led to divestiture due to evolving geopolitical issues in Russia and Ukraine. Additionally, Sylvamo discloses significant material adverse effects (MAE) that their business is subject to, and these are factored into our analysis throughout this paper. We seek to provide a financial analysis of Sylvamo Corporation through consideration of their 10-K in its entirety, as well as through ratio analysis. The company’s liquidity remains robust, with a current ratio of 1.8 and a quick ratio of 1.2, while gross and net profit margins of 20% and 3.8% leave room to enhance profitability. We review the CEO’s letter to shareholders and recommend product diversification, supply chain optimization, expansion into high-growth regions, streamlined operations, strategic rather than financial M&A, and increased investment in research and development. We conclude that Sylvamo represents a cautiously optimistic investment for investors with a long-term focus seeking moderate but stable returns.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether competition law can discipline Kenya's single-buyer electricity market and the state's vertical integration within it. detail.abstract: I present a theory of belief updating that integrates recency bias and salience theory into the Kalman filter. Recency bias modulates a dynamic, path-dependent subjective anchor with past information, while salience theory shapes the adjustment of the current surprise relative to this anchor. My framework provides a structural foundation for several empirical puzzles, including the dynamics of job search effort, the momentum-plateau-reversal transition, the background contrast effect, and the "buy on rumors, sell on facts" strategy. By decomposing belief overreaction into lagged, recency-biased, and salience-driven components, I illuminate the inertia of overreaction, explaining the long-term reversal and the limits of arbitrage in financial markets. Finally, a comparative statics analysis reveals that the recency-biased and salience-driven overreactions respond in fundamentally different, and often opposing, ways to key parameters.

title: The Natural Law: A Coherent Moral Theory of the State

detail.abstract: In this paper, we seek to understand whether the Christian conception of natural law is indispensable to a coherent moral theory of the state. Through an analysis of natural law thinkers beginning with Plato and Aristotle and continuing through Cicero, Augustine, Aquinas, Luther and Hooker, Calvin, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, and finally Rawls, we arrive at the conclusion that morally cohesive societies are not possible without the Christian conception of natural law. We further argue that other forms of and precursors to natural law were imperfect and required different mechanisms to operate optimally for the benefit of those who make up the polis. Therefore, we conclude that because pre-Christian natural law thinkers pointed toward the image of God and invoked a need for one, because the federal government has increasingly acted as a proxy for God, and because of the work of later natural law thinkers, a Christian conception of natural law is indispensable to a coherent moral theory of the state.

detail.abstract: This paper examines why transformative constitutions promise participation as a status while competition law can deliver it only as a market position. Comparing Kenya and South Africa, it proposes a participation ladder of access, stake and authority, and argues that South African merger control climbs the stake rung while neglecting authority, and that Kenya's statute barely leaves the ground. Ownership conditions risk nominal transfers; identity-based disadvantage categories invite capture in Kenya's ethnic politics. The paper therefore advances a functional test of disadvantage anchored in market dependence, staged remedies and reasoned monitoring, and tests it against merger, buyer-power and digital-inclusion practice.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether competition law can carry the social and environmental commitments of a constitution without losing discipline. Comparing Kenya, South Africa and Brazil, it advances a concept of constitutional absorption capacity, measured by normative density, statutory conduit and institutional carrier. South Africa's merger gateway absorbs constitutional values; Brazil's economic order promises more than its agency delivers; Kenya's text is rich while its statute lags. Recent merger decisions, including the Safaricom-Vodacom transaction, test the argument. The paper rejects efficiency monism and unbounded pluralism alike, and proposes a staged, reasoned and reviewable method for embedding public-interest objectives in market regulation.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we seek to show that while Ben Bernanke and Hank Paulson were both capable leaders during the Financial Crisis of 2009, they were not effective statesmen, since they did not follow a strong model of statesmanship of the kind described by Fischer (2020) and Stockman (2013). Through a lack of disclosure, Odyssean forward guidance, and other economic tools used by the leadership of the Federal Reserve and the Department of the Treasury, as well as the conduct of executive leadership at financial firms and their relationships with other members of the financial system, one can see that there is a clear need for transparency and accountability within the financial system. For this to occur, there need to be statesmen who recognize the power and authority of the Constitution, the rights afforded to citizens, the economic powers that the government does and does not have, and the response and intervention mechanisms that do exist. Intervention, when it occurs, should be consistent with the Constitution and with human flourishing. By studying Ben Bernanke, Hank Paulson, and the role of the banking system in the Financial Crisis of 2009, and by evaluating those actors and their behavior during the crisis, we can gain insight into how a Christian statesman can provide economic policy analysis that is proactive in nature and seeks to mitigate financial crises before regime change occurs.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether competition law can discipline the business of sport in Kenya and South Africa. Sports federations write rules. They also sell rights, license rivals and punish defectors. This combination is called regulatory custody here. The paper argues that custody, and not the sporting flavour of a rule, should trigger scrutiny. Both countries own effects-based competition statutes. Neither has produced a reasoned judgment on federation governance. South Africa holds an agents' cartel settlement, a refusal-to-supply ruling from pay television and an untested buyer power question about elite clubs. Kenya holds a broadcast-rights quarrel between its federation and its league, a complaint lodged with the Competition Authority, and a nine-month FIFA suspension. These events are read against the Court of Justice's 2023 rulings in ISU and European Superleague, and against Alston in the United States. The paper tests the claim that sporting autonomy ousts market scrutiny. The claim fails where a body regulates and trades without published, objective criteria. The paper then tests the opposite claim, that competition law alone can repair sport. That claim fails too, because enforcement capacity is thin and remedies are slow. A three-question custody screen follows. It asks whether a body regulates and trades, whether it gates access without a framework, and whether it can evidence a public interest justification. The screen is applied to broadcast rights, youth recruitment and sanctions. Concurrent jurisdiction protocols between competition and sports authorities are then proposed, together with a duty to publish reasons. Transformation objectives in South African law and consumer rights in Kenya's Constitution enter the screen as weights. The paper concludes that sport merits proportionate deference but never immunity, and that African regulators can lead rather than follow. Sport's commercial rise makes that leadership urgent, and the cost of delay falls on athletes, clubs and fans.

detail.abstract: Kenya stands at the threshold of enacting the Construction Payments Adjudication Bill, 2025, a statute that would, for the first time, place adjudicators at the centre of construction dispute resolution. Nevertheless, the Bill imports the language of impartiality and independence without confronting the structural conditions under which Kenyan adjudicators will actually operate: a shallow professional pool, overlapping institutional memberships, executive-dominated appointing authorities and an underdeveloped disclosure culture. This article interrogates the doctrinal architecture of bias, apparent bias and independence as developed in English, Canadian, East African Court of Justice and international arbitral jurisprudence, and tests its transplantability into the Kenyan construction sector. Drawing from Kenyan case law, the Fair Administrative Action Act 2015, the Arbitration Act 1995 and comparative statutory adjudication regimes, it argues that the orthodox fair-minded-observer test is necessary but insufficient absent structural safeguards calibrated to Kenya's thin adjudicator market. The article proposes a composite Kenyan standard combining the objective apprehension-of-bias test with mandatory, continuing disclosure, a statutorily insulated appointing body, and empirically grounded eligibility criteria, thereby making an original contribution to construction law scholarship in Africa.

detail.abstract: Multi-tenant cloud architecture has quietly dissolved the assumption, foundational to conflict-of-laws doctrine, that data possesses an ascertainable location. Where a single server hosts fragmented, sharded, and constantly migrating data belonging to dozens of unrelated tenants across several jurisdictions, disputes routinely implicate three or more sovereign legal orders at once, none of them decisively. This article argues that adjudicative models built on territorial jurisdiction and bilateral conflict-of-laws rules are structurally unsuited to genuinely multiparty cloud disputes, and proposes a mediation-centred Cloud Jurisdiction Protocol, adapted from multi-door justice theory and African dispute-resolution practice, as a more coherent institutional response.

title: New Deal Evaluation: American Leadership, Fiscal Rectitude, and Economic Outcomes with Respect to Statesmanship

detail.abstract: The lessons that we learn from economic and financial crises remain, notably, ex post: we examine crises after they unfold so that we can develop sound and specific financial policy guidance to help prevent future crises before they occur. In this paper we do this with respect to the interventions of the Great Depression, post-war fiscal consolidations, and the end of the gold standard. By analyzing the state of America during the 1930s and the decades that followed, we can inform the economic and political regime of the modern era (Stockman, 2013). We analyze the decisions and impacts of key government leaders during the New Deal, the Eisenhower administration, and the Nixon era, and we apply moral ethics to political and public choice economics and public policy. To accomplish this, we develop criteria by which statesmen who recognize the power and authority of the Constitution can establish policy that respects the rights and privileges afforded to citizens and act responsibly in the course of their duties. When intervention does occur, it should maximize human flourishing. The decisions of executive leadership cannot be considered in a vacuum; they must be considered alongside the banking industry’s role, and both should be evaluated using a model of limited government, justice, covenant, and non-centralized power (Fischer, 2020; Gwartney et al., 2022). It is not intervention itself that is bad; it is the manner and reasoning of intervention that must be examined carefully.

title: Presidential Comparison: Romney, Obama, and How Economic Policy Engendered Statism, Crony Capitalism, and Speculative Finance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we seek to answer the following question: How did Mitt Romney’s economic ideas, viewed in light of his role at Bain Capital, compare with those of President Obama, and what was the impact of President Obama’s economic policies especially via the Federal Reserve and his support for green energy, on economic statism, crony capitalism, and speculative financing? We argue that the 2012 election offered a sharper contrast in rhetoric than in substantive policy. Romney called for lower marginal rates, a cap on spending, and the repeal of Dodd-Frank and the Affordable Care Act, but his career in leveraged buyouts (LBOs), depended on the cheap credit that the Federal Reserve supplied, and his platform left that credit largely unaccounted for. We show that Obama’s stimulus, green energy loan guarantees, auto rescue, Dodd-Frank, and the near-zero interest rates and asset purchases of the Federal Reserve each moved economic decisions from the free market to the federal government, rewarded political connections, and encouraged investors to reach for yield. We evaluate both candidates through a biblical model of statesmanship that calls for limited and non-centralized government, impartial justice, honest measures, and stewardship that distinguishes production investment from speculative investment. We propose a statesmanlike response that is rules-based over discretion, bankruptcy consequences over bailouts, and austerity before tax cuts.

title: Truths in Tension: Liberalism, Conservatism, and Nationalism Under a Biblical Model of Statesmanship

detail.abstract: I compare classical liberalism, modern liberalism, and conservatism, as well as evaluate the benefits and costs of nationalism, and assess how these ideologies have shaped American policy and politics, with particular attention to economic and monetary policy. Drawing on Koyzis’ treatment of ideology as idolatry, Sowell’s critique of cosmic justice, and the scholarly literature on nationalism and macroeconomic policy, I argue that every one of these traditions grasps something true about the created order and turns harmful once that truth is given a sovereignty that belongs to only God. The analysis traces how Roosevelt’s positive rights entered federal law through the Employment Act of 1946 and the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate, how the long argument over whether central banks should follow rules or exercise discretion reflects older arguments about the limits of human knowledge, why the conflicting evidence on fiscal multipliers counsels humility, and how the 2018 tariffs placed much of their cost on the citizens they were meant to protect. The paper concludes with a biblical model of statesmanship built on five principles: the sovereignty of God, the image of God in every person, the division of power among fallen rulers, shared responsibility for the poor, and an ordered love of country.

detail.abstract: This article examines how the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) acquired, managed, and applied data across five major telecommunications infrastructure initiatives implemented between January 1996 and December 2025. Using a comparative case design that holds the implementing institution constant across five administrations, the study asks how FCC data practices shape movement from policy design to implementation. Two key findings emerged from this study. First, each case shows a design-to-implementation gap: identifiable decision points at which implementation choices modified, delayed, or departed from formal design, with outcomes ranging from full failure to successful launch or material but bounded divergence. Second, FCC data practices have repeatedly produced a fragmented, siloed information ecosystem marked by inconsistent definitions, non-interoperable systems, uncertain provider-reported inputs, and uneven coordination. This degrades the administrative visibility targeting, monitoring, and enforcement depend upon. Cross-case comparison indicates data fragmentation is a necessary but not sufficient condition for divergence: Organizational arrangements, not data quality alone, distinguished the single case that failed outright from the four that achieved full or partial convergence. National security recurred as a cross-cutting obligation in the cases (implicitly or explicitly) rather than a discrete policy stream. These findings suggest that closing the design-to-implementation gap in telecommunications policy requires attention to organizational structure alongside data infrastructure. This lays the groundwork for extending this single-agency analysis into the interagency landscape in which federal infrastructure policy actually operates.

detail.abstract: Leveraging spatial variation in dual concession jurisdictions, we show that accessibility shapes concession placement and the distribution of institutional authority, thereby influencing subsequent economic and financial development. Prior work attributes comparative advancement to the common law relative to the civil law. Our evidence, robust across multiple specifications, measures, and spatial adjustments, suggests that accessibility predicts concession placement, conditioning institutional exposure and, in turn, fostering economic and financial expansion. This mechanism identifies accessibility as a key factor structuring institutional reach and development, with continuing relevance for global economic and financial connectivity and implications for the scholarship on law and development.

title: Budziszewski’s Natural Law Jurisprudence and the Classical Foundations of Statesmanship
