detail.abstract: This review essay evaluates J. Budziszewski’s natural law framework, as presented in The Line Through the Heart, within the broader context of classical statesmanship and modern public policy. By synthesizing Budziszewski’s tripartite understanding of natural law as fact, theory, and sign of contradiction, with the foundational insights of Plato, Aristotle, and Cicero, this essay explores the ontological necessity of an objective moral standard discoverable by reason. The investigation critiques the "Second Tablet Project" and modern functionalism, arguing that a metaphysics of dignity grounded in the imago Dei is essential for protecting human personhood against utilitarian exploitation. Furthermore, it addresses the tension between teleological goodness and relational adaptation, proposing that republican constitutionalism offers a vital procedural framework for managing moral complexities in pluralistic societies. Finally, the essay applies these principles to contemporary dilemmas in bioethics and economic property rights, asserting the enduring relevance of the "law written on the heart" for the maintenance of a just and stable political order.

title: A Review and Discussion of Hill’s After the Natural Law: How the Classical Worldview Supports Our Modern Moral and Political Values

detail.abstract: This essay provides a comprehensive review and critical discussion of John Lawrence Hill’s After the Natural Law: How the Classical Worldview Supports Our Modern Moral and Political Values (2016). Hill’s central thesis posits that the modern Western crisis of values stems from a "profound amnesia" regarding the teleological and metaphysical foundations of the classical worldview. The analysis traces the historical trajectory of natural law from the classical synthesis of Augustine and Aquinas through the Protestant Reformation (through the continuity of natural law in the thought of Luther, Calvin, and Hooker) to the "Great Retreat" into nominalism and materialism discussed by Ockham, Hobbes, and Locke. By integrating contemporary scholarship from J. Budziszewski and Thomas Pogge, this review evaluates the practical application of natural law principles to modern public policy challenges, including the protection of human life, global economic justice, and the ethics of public health lockdowns. While acknowledging critiques regarding Hill’s emphasis on ontological free will, the paper concludes that a revitalized natural law tradition is essential for providing a coherent foundation for human dignity, personal responsibility, and the rule of law in a pluralistic age.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the position of regions in the European inter-regional network of production and trade shaped their resilience to the Great Recession and the sovereign debt crisis, focusing on two dimensions of resilience: resistance and recovery. Using pre-crisis interregional input–output flows, we measure the network centrality of European NUTS2 regions and compare the GDP per capita and employment trajectories of highly central regions with those of comparable regions with low centrality, relative to the last pre-crisis year. Highly central regions showed weaker resistance, in the form of a deeper decline, and a slower return to their pre-crisis levels. When centrality is measured on the economy-wide network, their gap relative to comparable regions widened until 2013–2014, reaching 7–9 per cent of GDP per capita and 3.4–4.2 percentage points of the employment rate, and had narrowed only marginally by 2015. While GDP per capita in low-centrality regions was back above its pre-crisis level by 2010, highly central regions regained it only in 2014, and their employment rate was still below its pre-crisis level in 2015. No systematic effects emerge for regions with intermediate centrality, and effects are stronger when centrality reflects the whole economy rather than manufacturing alone. These findings challenge the assumption that regional connectivity uniformly fosters resilience, showing that the risks of interdependence are concentrated among the most central regions. Overall, the study highlights that network position is a key structural determinant of regional vulnerability to systemic shocks, offering novel insights for targeted policy interventions.

title: Natural Law, Economic Inequality, and the Administrative State: A Policy Memorandum
affiliations: Grand Canyon University

detail.abstract: This policy memorandum analyzes economic inequality and the growth of the modern administrative state through the lens of natural law. We argue that the departure from natural law theory, traced from Aristotle, Zeno of Citium, and Thomas Aquinas through the social-contract thought of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau, has left modern policy without an objective metaphysical anchor for human dignity and rights, and that this gap is part of why policy intervention is now required. Drawing on Budziszewski (2011) and Hill (2016), the memorandum contends that economic reform should be reoriented around objective moral truths rather than a shifting general will. It engages the double-distortion argument in the law-and-economics debate over inequality (Dimick, 2016) and the evidence that carefully targeted interventions, tested through randomized controlled trials, can work (Awoa Awoa et al., 2024; Banerjee & Duflo, 2007). We then recommend a course of action for lawmakers: reject the double-distortion premise that efficiency and equity are independent; ask state universities to conduct regional economic studies so that problems can be addressed locally and granularly; protect property rights as a foundation of natural law; and reform labor and wage policy on the premise that every person is endowed with inherent dignity. The goal is to improve the economic lives of citizens in the United States while limiting government overreach.

title: The Hamiltonian Roots of Modern Monetary Intervention
affiliations: Grand Canyon University

detail.title: The Hamiltonian Roots of Modern Monetary Intervention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: In this analysis, I introduce the research area of economic policy through an analysis of the primary source literature surrounding the founding of the United States. Through an analysis of secondary sources that contextually frame these primary documents, we can engage with the literature in an authoritative way to understand the constructivist argumentation that anchors policy. I interrogate the literature and find that the Commerce Clause and the General Welfare Clause allow for government intervention so long as it provides for the general welfare. Specifically, the Commerce Clause serves as the method by which this occurs through the management of liquidity. Alexander Hamilton’s advocacy for an expansive federal government remains emblematic of the powers Congress was eventually able to extend as a consequence of McCulloch v. Maryland. It is through this lens of intervention that I frame the specific policy question of how consumption and labor market outcomes respond to unexpected monetary policy shocks in downturns versus expansions. By understanding Hamiltonian monetary policy as a foundational precursor to Keynesian investment economics, we can better contextualize the evolutionary flow of broader monetary intervention.

detail.abstract: Sylvamo Corporation (SLVM), a global leader in the uncoated papers industry, operates paper mills and a portfolio of paper brands. Operating in a highly competitive market dominated by a few major players, Sylvamo’s growth strategy is underpinned by mergers and acquisitions aimed at enhancing market share and operational efficiencies. This paper conducts a comprehensive valuation of Sylvamo, applying three distinct methodologies: the income approach (discounted cash flow), the market approach (valuation multiples), and the asset-based approach (adjusted net assets). The analysis encompasses the identification and evaluation of nonoperating and excess assets, as well as a detailed risk assessment incorporating applicable discounts and premiums to reflect Sylvamo’s assumed status as a private entity. The results from the three approaches are reconciled to derive a final value estimate, which is subsequently compared to Sylvamo’s market capitalization as of the most recent financial reporting period. Based on the valuation gap and market conditions, the paper concludes with a buy/sell recommendation supported by detailed analysis.

detail.abstract: Sylvamo Corporation, spun off from International Paper in 2021, is a global producer of uncoated papers and market pulp. This paper analyzes Sylvamo’s business using its 10-K and 10-Q filings, focusing on its internal and external environment, competitive strengths and weaknesses, and economic outlook. Its strengths include well-known brands such as Hammermill, a diversified product portfolio, and an extensive distribution network across North America, Latin America, and Europe; its weaknesses center on volatile raw material and energy costs. The analysis identifies the long-term decline in office paper demand caused by digitalization as the principal threat, alongside competition from Domtar, Sappi, and Asia Pulp & Paper, stringent environmental regulation, exposure to commodity prices and exchange rates, and possible changes in corporate tax policy. It also examines how GDP growth, inflation, and interest rates shape demand and operating costs. Growth opportunities lie in emerging markets, particularly Latin America, where demand for printed materials remains stable, and in sustainability-oriented products. Taken together, these factors yield a holistic view of Sylvamo’s strategic path, highlighting both opportunities for expansion and significant risks that could impede future growth.

detail.abstract: This report examines Sylvamo Corporation’s financial performance over fiscal years 2019–2023, using its 10-K filings to analyze common-size income statements, financial ratios, and cash flow trends, and it asks what financial benefits transparent disclosure can bring to a company and its shareholders. The common-size analysis shows cost of sales rising from 69.8 percent of net revenue in 2020 to 75.5 percent in 2023, compressing gross margin from 30.2 to 24.5 percent, while the net margin peaked at 9.5 percent in 2021 before falling to 6.8 percent in 2023. Liquidity strengthened, with the current ratio improving from 1.39 in 2019 to 1.71 in 2023, and the debt ratio held near 60 percent, although times interest earned declined to 7.8 and returns on equity and assets fell. Operating cash flow averaged $431 million a year and funded investment and shareholder returns. Drawing on research linking disclosure quality to market valuation, shareholder returns, and the value of cash holdings, we argue that clear and accurate financial reporting is worth the effort it requires. The findings emphasize the company’s operational resilience, its challenges with rising costs, and strategies for balancing growth with financial discipline.

title: Financial Ratio Analysis of Honeywell International Inc.

detail.abstract: Financial ratio analysis converts accounting numbers into relative indicators that reveal a firm’s liquidity, efficiency, leverage, profitability and cash‑flow health. By comparing line items within and across financial statements, ratios illuminate trends that raw figures obscure. This study examines Honeywell International Inc.’s financial performance during fiscal 2022–2024 using a spreadsheet model to compute common liquidity, activity, solvency, profitability and cash‑flow ratios. Drawing on scholarly literature, including a historical survey of ratio analysis (Horrigan, 1968), a recent systematic review (Zhang et al., 2025) and a comparative analysis of traditional and cash‑flow ratios (Seretidou et al., 2025), the report explains the purpose and limitations of ratio analysis and integrates faith‑based reflections on stewardship and integrity. The results show that Honeywell maintained robust liquidity and profitability while increasing leverage and experiencing a modest decline in asset utilisation. Cash‑flow ratios confirm strong operating and free cash flow. The analysis underscores the enduring value of ratio analysis for financial management but notes that it is inherently retrospective and should be complemented with forward‑looking methods. Faith integration highlights how ethical financial stewardship aligns with biblical principles.

title: Business Valuation: Comparing and Contrasting Different Approaches
affiliations: Grand Canyon University

detail.abstract: There are three main methods of valuing a private company: the income approach, the asset approach, and the market approach. This paper compares and contrasts them, arguing that the appropriate method is the one that highlights the strengths of the subject company and minimizes the weaknesses of the valuation, within industry norms. Following Hitchner (2017), the income approach is probably the most widely recognized and utilized approach, and its central tool, the discounted cash flow (DCF) method, continues to be refined, for example through an analytical solution to the circularity problem (Mejía-Peláez & Vélez-Pareja, 2011). The asset approach, based on the value of tangible assets less liabilities, is a natural basis for asset-heavy or liquidation scenarios, but it does not capture future growth potential. The market approach is relative, relying on comparable transactions and valuation multiples such as P/E and EV/EBITDA; it reflects market perception and can be difficult to apply to unique or niche businesses that lack comparables, although normalization can reduce some discrepancies. The paper also considers when analysts prefer each method, the role of key performance indicators and financial risk, and the analyst’s duty to report accurately and transparently.

detail.abstract: This paper explores the significant challenges that valuation analysts face when assessing private companies, with a focus on comparability and industry standards. Valuations are essential for various business activities such as mergers, acquisitions, liquidations, and shareholder disputes. A well-reasoned valuation includes estimating future economic benefits and assessing the likelihood of their realization and long-term sustainability (Hitchner, 2017). Private companies often present unique difficulties due to a lack of comparable companies and irregular financial reporting practices. These challenges arise from complex situations and managerial discretion in financial reporting, necessitating adjustments and normalization of financial statements. The paper discusses the importance of comparative analysis through ratio analyses and common-size financial statements, despite obstacles in obtaining reliable data from private entities (Droj, Kwartnik-Pruc, & Droj, 2024). Emphasizing integrity and honesty, the discussion aligns with biblical principles as highlighted in 2 Kings, underscoring the ethical responsibilities of valuation analysts. Overcoming these challenges is not just routine for valuation professionals but is fundamental to providing accurate and relevant valuations that are crucial in financial and legal contexts.

title: Units as Stabilizations: Relational Constitution, Critical Ethology, and a Non-Substantialist Ethics of Method
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Units as Stabilizations: Relational Constitution, Critical Ethology, and a Non-Substantialist Ethics of Method

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is about Methodology and Philosophy of Social Sciences.
declarations.funderStatement: This work is not funded by any.

detail.abstract:
This paper begins from a practical and philosophical problem. Research and policy often treat categories, institutions, organisms and persons as self-explanatory objects rather than as outcomes of ongoing processes. In doing so they risk a narrative trap: maintained arrangements come to appear as natural facts, the practices that sustain them disappear from view, and people can come to identify wholly with the categories applied to them. A social science that aims at liberation may therefore help stabilize the very order it seeks to question.
The paper proposes that many units in the social and life sciences are better understood as stabilizations: units individuated within, and persisting through, maintained arrangements of relations. This claim is restricted to a domain-level thesis and does not require a general doctrine that reality is fundamentally relational. Three claims are distinguished throughout: an ontological claim that individuation is often relationally constituted; a performative claim that research, measurement and policy practices help maintain the units they describe; and a normative claim, introduced as an explicit commitment rather than a deduction, that stabilizations should be judged by their revisability and by who bears their exclusions.
The ontological thesis is defended through an argument from relational individuation that distinguishes identity-, persistence- and existence-dependence while openly identifying its grounding-essence bridge as a contestable premise. The paper argues that its empirical and ethical programmes require less than full acceptance of that bridge: the methodological framework depends primarily on claims about maintenance and persistence, while the ethics requires only grounded forms of dependence. The argument is further constrained by a distinction between relational constitution and determination, preserving a place for agency, and by a two-part invariance test that separates relationalism from relativism.
On this basis the paper develops critical ethology, a six-step research programme that treats social units as maintained stabilizations and compares relational, bearer-centred and hybrid explanations through pre-registered measures and perturbation-based inquiry. The method is illustrated through a prospective study design concerning caste classification while remaining applicable beyond that case. Because the protocol also treats research practices as stabilizing forces, the performative claim is applied reflexively to the method itself.

The paper concludes by proposing a non-substantialist ethics organized around constitutive standing, revisability and remainder accountability. Its central claim is not that stable categories are undesirable, but that categories on which liberty and equality of opportunity depend should remain open to contestation. The resulting framework links ontology, method and ethics through a single conditional chain: categories are maintained rather than given; research participates in their maintenance; therefore their persistence should be investigated empirically and their consequences evaluated ethically, while keeping both the categories and the inquiry that studies them open to revision

detail.abstract: This study develops an integrated three-year forecast of Honeywell International Inc.’s income statement and balance sheet for fiscal years 2025–2027. Following the forecasting principles in Tjia (2018), which emphasize consistency with historical performance, ratio-based projection of statement items, and avoidance of false precision, the model derives its assumptions from Honeywell’s FY2024 common-size statements and benchmarks them against management’s 2025 guidance. Revenue grows from an FY2024 base of $38.5 billion at 6 percent in 2025 and 2026 and 5 percent in 2027; cost of goods sold, selling, general and administrative expense, and research and development are held at their historical shares of revenue; interest expense, taxes, capital expenditure, and the composition of assets and liabilities are likewise projected as percentages of revenue; and dividends follow a stable 35 percent payout ratio, consistent with Lintner’s (1956) evidence on dividend smoothing. The forecast shows revenue of $40.8 billion in 2025, in line with guidance; net income to common rising from $5.47 billion in 2025 to $6.09 billion in 2027, with margins of roughly 13–14 percent; and total assets growing from $79.7 billion to $88.7 billion, with a current ratio near 1.4 and a debt-to-equity ratio near 3:1. The paper closes by relating this plan-before-you-build approach to a biblical ethic of stewardship.

detail.abstract: Success is often judged by visible outcomes such as educational attainment, career progression, financial security, or public recognition, but a fuller account also considers meaning, well-being, relationships, and adaptation. This narrative review synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature on purpose, goal setting, persistence, self-efficacy, deliberate practice, growth mindset, and lifelong learning. Rather than estimating pooled effects, it compares findings from foundational studies, longitudinal research, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. The synthesis suggests that purpose can help people prioritize meaningful aims; persistence can sustain effort when paired with feedback and strategic flexibility; and continuous learning can support skill development and adaptation. These processes are reinforced by realistic goals, social support, recovery, and access to learning opportunities. Evidence also qualifies popular success narratives: grit is not a complete or especially powerful standalone predictor, growth-mindset interventions do not consistently improve achievement, and associations between purpose and outcomes do not prove causation. The article proposes a six-stage framework linking values clarification, goal translation, action, focused practice, reflection, and support. Because the review did not use an exhaustive, reproducible search protocol and the framework has not been tested as an integrated intervention, it should be treated as an evidence-informed guide rather than a validated formula for success. AI assistance disclosure. Generative AI was used to assist with editorial review, language refinement, figure redrawing, and manuscript formatting. The author is responsible for verifying the references, reviewing the final text, and approving the submitted version. No new empirical data or experimental results were generated for this article.

detail.abstract: Liquidity management is one of the central tasks of managerial finance, yet the static measures most often used to assess it, such as the current and quick ratios, capture only a single moment and ignore the timing of cash flows. This paper examines working-capital management through the cash conversion cycle (CCC) of Richards and Laughlin (1980), which combines days inventory outstanding, days receivables outstanding, and days payables outstanding into a dynamic measure of how quickly a firm turns its investment in operations back into cash. Drawing on Cagle, Campbell, and Jones (2013), a 2024 PwC Middle East estimate that about US$50 billion of liquidity is trapped on the balance sheets of listed companies in the region, and recent professional guidance on receivables, payables, inventory, and cash forecasting, the paper argues that working capital should be managed proactively rather than merely measured. It then integrates a Christian worldview, drawing on Scripture’s teaching on planning (Luke 14:28; Proverbs 16:9), honesty and justice toward others (Proverbs 3:27; James 5:4; Romans 13:7), and faithful stewardship (Luke 16:10; 1 Peter 4:10). The paper concludes that ethical working-capital policies, which avoid cosmetic manipulation of liquidity ratios and treat suppliers, employees, and customers justly, are both sound finance and an expression of Christian stewardship.

detail.abstract: An et al. (2024) report a stronger disposition effect in loss portfolios and attribute it to portfolio-level mental accounting. We show that measuring performance from current holdings can generate this finding. Realized gains drop out, while retained losses remain, concentrating disposition-prone investors in loss portfolios. In matched samples, loss-portfolio investors' prior disposition effects are at least six times those of gain-portfolio investors. A model formalizes this sorting; simulations reproduce nearly two-thirds of the reported stock-portfolio gain interaction without portfolio-dependent selling. In experiments, including realized outcomes yields a precisely estimated zero interaction. These findings undermine the portfolio-level mental accounting explanation.

detail.abstract: Data-intensive forecasting models require longer and broader histories than most option markets can provide. This paper examines whether a model trained on US equity options can improve implied-volatility forecasts in smaller equity option markets, whether applied with its weights unchanged (zero-shot) or adapted to local data through fine-tuning, pooled training or forecast combination, relative to the same model trained on local data alone. Implied-volatility surfaces are constructed from raw exchange files for the US, Brazilian, Indian, Hong Kong and Canadian equity option markets, and a mixture-of-experts recurrent network forecasts, from each underlying's recent surface history, the two-week change in constant-maturity implied total variance net of the mechanical roll along the term structure. On a score that removes the credit for anticipating the reversal of quote noise, the best US-informed model improves on the local model in every market, by 1.1 to 3.7 points of skill over the walk-forward test years 2023-25 and by 0.5 to 6.7 points in a 2026 holdout year; a model selected on validation data before each test year beats the local model in all four markets over 2023-25, with blockbootstrap intervals that exclude zero in each, and the gains are stable across training seeds. Over 2023-25 the networks also outperform simple ridge, term-slope and gradient-boosting benchmarks, which themselves almost always forecast better when fitted on US data than on local data, although in 2026 simple rules beat the networks in three of the four target markets. The transferred model carries a term-structure rule that small local samples identify only weakly, and it is less exposed to local measurement noise than models estimated on local prices. The depth of a single large market can therefore compensate for the short histories of smaller ones, extending data-intensive forecasting models, so far applied predominantly to US options, to markets in which they could not be estimated reliably on their own.

detail.abstract: Temperature shocks transmit unevenly across consumer prices, with adjustment extending into services and unfolding over several months. This paper combines gridded ERA5-Land temperature data with 17 Harmonised Indices of Consumer Prices in 34 European countries over 2000-2025. Monthly local projections trace price-level responses to country-specific maximumtemperature anomalies over 24 months. Headline prices and services respond gradually, reaching 0.157% and 0.122% at month 20 for a one-country-standard-deviation shock. Larger late-horizon responses appear in alcoholic beverages, tobacco, and narcotics and in personal care, social protection, and miscellaneous goods and services. Several delayed positive responses persist across seven lag-history specifications. The patterns are consistent with temperature-induced supply pressures transmitted through sectors with heterogeneous price adjustment. These findings connect the supply effects of temperature to the literature on sectoral price rigidity and inform the assessment of climate-related inflation risks.

detail.abstract: A productive asset can remain worth operating after it has ceased to offer a feasible path to recovering its initial investment. This paper examines that distinction when technological change erodes project revenue from the investment date, while revenue generation begins only after deployment is complete. A deterministic model separates the operating-opportunity deadline, the effective recovery deadline, and the first recovery time. With fixed investment and operating parameters, when economic exit is the binding deadline, faster revenue erosion delays internal recovery and advances economic exit. Deployment introduces both forgone early operating cash flow and additional absorption expenditure. When absorption accelerates, deterioration in the deployment-to-opportunity ratio alone does not establish a decline in recovery value: a cash-flowweighted condition is also required. Under constant absorption speed, initial recoverability, and the further conditions of Proposition A.6, including strictly increasing net erosion tending to infinity and a binding potential-profitability cutoff throughout, the recovery threshold occurs before operating opportunity disappears and before the corresponding threshold for otherwise identical immediate operation. The recovery criterion is equivalent to nonnegative truncated NPV under the same execution policy, costs, deadline, and zero-terminal-value convention. The contribution is a decomposition of project timing and conditional comparative statics, rather than a new valuation principle or a general claim that AI investment destroys value. Numerical examples illustrate the thresholds; an empirical design identifies the data and assumptions needed to investigate them.

detail.abstract: International reserve demand is global, while the institutions supporting reserve assets remain predominantly national. This paper develops a Global Reserve Bank issuing settlement balances and reserve securities denominated in an International Dollar. The proposal preserves national currencies and separates international reserve services from domestic monetary stabilization. Its contribution is a contractual framework linking reserve demand, asset pooling, currency-specific liquidity, limited sovereign support, and voluntary participation. A replication benchmark establishes that relabeling existing payoffs adds no opportunity under frictionless access. A pooling result identifies when enforceable transfers expand statewise support capacity without creating aggregate wealth. A reservechoice model derives instrument demand from payment shortfalls, and a constrained issuance problem equates marginal service value with operating, liquidity, and support costs. The analysis distinguishes denomination from backing, liquidity loans from capital, and nominal guarantees from credible contributions. A reproducible numerical illustration using artificial inputs shows that common support can expand feasible issuance while optimal issuance remains below that boundary. Operating costs can reverse the welfare ranking, and an equivalent lower-cost decentralized network can dominate a common issuer. The institutional case is therefore conditional on enforceability, additional service value, and participation. The paper offers a specified alternative for organizing international monetary commitments rather than an empirical estimate of its benefits or a claim that a new currency eliminates national fiscal constraints.

detail.abstract: Most life annuities sold in the United States carry a period-certain guarantee: if the annuitant dies early, the remaining payments go to a named beneficiary. Whether the beneficiary actually collects is uncertain. Heirs may not know the contract exists, deaths may go undetected, and unclaimed amounts are eventually escheated to the state. We introduce this beneficiary settlement risk into a life-cycle model in which a retiree allocates wealth among a liquid asset, a life-only annuity and a period-certain annuity. Insurers remain liable for the guarantee, so premiums do not depend on settlement, but heirs receive it only with probability π. We show that uncertain settlement is a lottery rather than a haircut, derive a closed-form threshold for π below which no guarantee is bought, and bound the welfare cost by the option value of the guarantee. In a calibration to U.S. mortality and market payout ratios, lowering π from one to one-half reduces the period-certain share of wealth from 44% to 2% for a retiree with moderate bequest motives; life-only annuities absorb most of the change, and total annuitization falls by at most 9 percentage points. Welfare costs are small for households that re-optimize and up to four times larger for those that keep their guarantee. Unlike insurer default risk of the same expected size, settlement risk leaves life-only annuitants and money's-worth ratios unaffected and changes the mix rather than the level of annuity demand.

detail.abstract:
Economic sanctions may impose immediate costs while contributing to responses that alter capabilities, dependencies, and future policy options. This manuscript develops the Sanctions–Adaptation–Targeting Doctrine, a conditional framework for assessing these effects across time without treating economic damage as sufficient evidence of success or adaptation as proof of failure.

The framework combines objective-specific policy assessment, functional substitution analysis, institutional-learning tests, and independent legal analysis. A structured comparison of Russia, Ukraine, and Wildberries distinguishes national conditions, organizational arrangements, specified capabilities, and facility-specific incidents. It examines whether restrictions contribute to capability preservation, alternative networks, changed military reliance upon commercial infrastructure, or broader targeting claims.

Three proposed mechanisms—the Third-State Learning Externality, Adaptive Exposure Paradox, and Targeting-Precedent Externality—require separate evidence of transmission, changed practices, performance, and consequences. Observation does not establish learning; alternative networks do not establish fragmentation; and rhetorical invocation does not establish operational adoption. Commercial military reliance, military-objective classification, and attack legality remain distinct inquiries. Another belligerent’s conduct supplies no automatic legal permission.

The resulting Adaptation-Adjusted Sanctions Effectiveness Framework compares outcomes against specified objectives, time horizons, and feasible alternatives while accounting for civilian consequences, coalition cooperation, continuing dependencies, and credible relief. Its contribution is an inspectable method for connecting economic statecraft, infrastructure exposure, and diplomatic reassessment. The doctrine proposes neither a universal causal sequence nor a validated forecasting model; it identifies what must be demonstrated before longer-term strategic consequences can be attributed to economic pressure.

detail.abstract:
In this paper, we analyse an approximation to the switch value of a Bermudan swaption. The approximation is calculated solely from the details of the corresponding European swaptions but independent of the actual European swaption pricing model and its model assumptions. This settings allows for a direct application of the method to non-standard Bermudan swaptions.

The purpose of the approximation is to assess the materiality of the switch value relative to the corresponding maximum-European swaption price. Such an assessment can inform the model user, for example, whether an approximation of the Bermudan swaption price by the maximum European swaption price is fit for purpose in a pricing or risk management context.

A guiding principle of the approximation is simplicity. We do not aim for a particularly accurate approximation to the switch value of the original model. Nevertheless, our numerical case studies demonstrate that the method produces reasonable switch value approximations.

detail.abstract: This paper compares a popular-press commentary on recent U.S. fiscal policy (Bunn, 2026) with an academic analysis of the 2018 tariffs (Amiti et al., 2019) to evaluate which qualifies as scientific inquiry. Using Walliman’s (2020) account of the scientific method (identifying and clarifying problems, formulating hypotheses, testing them, and eliminating or adjusting unsuccessful solutions) and four philosophy-of-science frameworks (positivism, interpretivism, Weber’s reconciliatory approach, and Bhaskar’s critical realism), the paper shows that the academic article, grounded in replicable methods, explicit hypotheses, prior literature, and transparent sourcing, meets the criteria for scientific inquiry. The popular article, by contrast, relies on an emotive headline and rhetorical framing, draws its evidence almost entirely from analyses produced by the organization its author leads, and does not address published criticism of that organization’s materials; it is therefore best classified as personal exposition rather than science. The paper then proposes research questions on the size and targeting of direct stimulus payments after COVID-19, building on Osuoha (2022), and explains why they are testable with quantitative methods. Finally, it situates the research within a biblical worldview that encourages testing and rigorous inquiry and holds that Scripture and science do not conflict.

title: Puppy Federalism or Structural Safeguard? Rubin, Thomas, and the Relevance of the Founders’ Federalism
affiliations: Grand Canyon University

detail.abstract: Is the federalism established by the Founders still relevant? This paper reviews and compares two influential short essays that answer the question differently. Edward Rubin (2001) separates federalism, which gives subunits definitive rights against the central government, from decentralization, a management strategy the center chooses for its own purposes, and argues that because the United States now enjoys strong national unity, what remains is “puppy federalism” that looks like the real thing but lacks its substance. Justice Clarence Thomas (2000), in his Dwight D. Opperman Lecture, argues instead that federalism, like the separation of powers, is a structural safeguard for individual liberty grounded in the Founders’ realistic view of human nature. The paper assesses each essay’s method, strengths, and weaknesses and then synthesizes them. It argues that Thomas has the stronger case, because the purpose of federalism was never only to protect regional identity but to restrain concentrated power, a purpose that has not changed, while Rubin’s critique remains valuable for showing how easily federalism becomes rhetoric when its limits are not enforced. The Federal Reserve’s regional structure illustrates Rubin’s distinction between federalism and decentralization, and recent divergence among the states suggests that, by Rubin’s own test, genuine federalism may again be necessary.

detail.abstract: Emerging markets with high levels of inequality tend to have fewer capital controls. We propose a novel dynamic real-exchange-rate distributional externality as a potential explanation of this pattern. We develop a small open economy model with nonhomothetic preferences, high-income borrowers subject to an occasionally binding collateral constraint, and low-income hand-to-mouth households. Borrowing generates an intertemporal distributional externality through the real exchange rate. A planner can improve redistribution by manipulating the terms of trade in favor of the poor. We decompose the optimal borrowing tax into Fisherian and distributional components. Quantitatively, incorporating inequality can lower the average optimal macroprudential tax substantially and even turn it into a subsidy. We extend our framework to a production economy and show that our mechanism remains quantitatively significant as long as wages are flexible.

detail.abstract: Competition remedies targeting individual product markets often operate within platform ecosystems shaped by complementary services and cooperation across markets. We examine how these relationships condition the effects of browser choice screens on iPhones. Introduced under the EU Digital Markets Act in 2024, these screens require consumers to actively choose a default browser. We compare browser and search market shares in EU and non-EU countries before and after the rollout. We find a substantial shift in market share from the dominant browser Safari to Google Chrome, and document small absolute gains for other browsers. These effects varied systematically with pre-intervention ecosystem presence: Safari lost less market share in countries with greater desktop Safari use, while Chrome gained more where the Google ecosystem was more established. In the complementary search market, which monetizes browser traffic, the effect on Google's market share was negligible, since Google remains the default search engine in both browsers. Our findings suggest that ecosystem complementarities and cooperation across markets can limit the reach of product market remedies even when the targeted market responds substantially.

detail.abstract: In the present study an attempt has been made to study the interrelationships and volatility dynamics of selected Indian and global financial and commodity indicators namely Bitcoin, Brent Oil, Dow Jones, Gold, Indian 10-year government bond yield (IND10Y), NSE NIFTY 50, US 10-year government bond yield (USA10Y) and USD-INR currency pair. The statistical characteristics and relationships between the selected indicators are investigated by means of descriptive statistics, Karl Pearson’s correlation coefficients, stationarity tests and multicollinearity diagnostics. Then six GARCH family models (GARCH, EGARCH, PARCH, CGARCH, FIGARCH and FIEGARCH) are estimated to check the relationships and volatility dynamics of three selected dependent indicators (IND10Y, NSE NIFTY 50 and USD-INR). The empirical results suggest that all the selected indicators are stationary at level and the multicollinearity is not a serious problem. The analysis of correlations shows that the selected indicators are more or less associated with each other, but no strong correlations were found. The GARCH estimation results reveal significant relationships between Brent Oil, USA10Y and NSE NIFTY 50 with IND10Y; Dow Jones, Bitcoin, Gold, IND10Y and USD-INR with NSE NIFTY 50; and Gold, NSE NIFTY 50 and IND10Y with USD-INR currency pair. Moreover, the comparison of model-fit statistics, residual properties, diagnostic tests, and forecasting performance shows that the appropriateness of GARCH family models varies across the selected financial indicators. CGARCH(1,1) performs better for USD-INR under these criteria while Conventional GARCH(1,1) shows better performance in terms of explanatory power and residual-based measures for IND10Y and NSE NIFTY 50. In contrast, information criteria indicate the FIGARCH(1,1) model is a better specification for IND10Y and USD-INR, while EGARCH(1,1) is the best for NSE NIFTY 50. The forecasting results also show that FIGARCH(1,1) outperforms other competing models across several evaluation measures, particularly for IND10Y and USD-INR, whereas conventional GARCH(1,1) shows favorable performance for NSE NIFTY 50. The overall results show that none of the GARCH specifications outperforms the others for all the indicators and criteria of evaluation chosen. The results provide useful insights into the interrelationships, volatility behavior and forecasting performance of Indian and global financial and commodity markets.

detail.abstract: Hunger persists despite unprecedented levels of global food production. In many modern economies, food insecurity is increasingly a problem of access rather than supply. Millions of individuals struggle to secure reliable meals, while restaurants and other food-service providers frequently operate below capacity. This coexistence of unmet nutritional needs and underutilized productive resources suggests a structural market coordination failure. This paper introduces Universal Meal Rights (UMR) and proposes Universal Meal Insurance (UMI) as a new institutional framework for guaranteeing access to ordinary daily meals. Unlike conventional welfare programs based on means-testing, UMI treats meal access as a universal social right. The system is implemented through Meal-Specific Purpose-Oriented Currency (Meal-PoC), a non-transferable, non-accumulable, and automatically expiring monetary instrument redeemable exclusively for ordinary meals. The paper further develops a model of capacity-constrained monetary issuance, in which MealPoC creation is linked to the productive capacity of restaurants, cafeterias, and food supply networks. By connecting purchasing power directly to available meal-producing capacity, the framework seeks to expand access while limiting inflationary pressures. More broadly, the paper reframes meals as a form of economic infrastructure rather than a welfare benefit. By combining universal rights, purpose-oriented currency, market-based delivery, and capacity-constrained issuance, it proposes a new market-design approach to food security capable of reducing hunger, improving affordability, and strengthening local food economies in an age of abundance.

detail.abstract: We propose a framework for understanding and evaluating recursive self-improvement (RSI) leaning in artificial intelligence systems. RSI refers to the ability of AI systems to iteratively improve their capabilities and performance through successive cycles of feedback and self-modification. As one of the paths to AGI without a unified definition, we propose a hierarchical framework for defining RSI based on the extent to which a system improves its own learning mechanisms and the degree to which a system can independently identify opportunities, develop strategies, and execute improvements. This framework aims to establish a common language for evaluating RSI capabilities and understanding the potential pathways through which AI systems can progressively enhance their own intelligence.

detail.abstract:
Water underpins life and economic activity, yet its contribution remains largely overlooked in standard economic indicators such as the GDP. Moreover, although the UK Office for National Statistics publishes annual Natural Capital Accounts, water-related ecosystems remain underrepresented. This study addresses the methodological and practical challenges of compiling water ecosystem condition accounts consistent with the System of Environmental Economic Accounting–Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA-EA) framework and assesses their relevance for informing water policy.

Using England as a case study, we develop water condition accounts using three complementary indicators: ecological status under the Water Framework Directive, and riverine nitrate and Escherichia coli (E. coli) concentrations modelled using a detailed water quality model. Results show that nitrate concentrations remain consistently below the regulatory threshold of 11.3 mg N/L across all regions and years, indicating generally good nutrient conditions, although London exhibits comparatively higher levels. In contrast, E. coli concentrations, based on the 90th percentile of bathing-season (May–September) values, display substantial spatial and temporal variability. All regions consistently exceed the regulatory threshold of 9 colony forming units (CFU)/mL across the examined period (2004–2018). The North West records by far the highest 90th percentile values, reaching around 146 CFU/mL in some years, while the South West consistently shows the lowest concentrations, generally in the range of 19–25 CFU/mL.

By comparing ecosystem condition accounts with existing policy monitoring frameworks, the study shows how systematically developed water condition accounts can improve coherence across indicators and support more effective water management decisions.

detail.title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.

title: How Much Growth Does a Higher VAT Threshold Allow? Evidence from a Large Increase in Romania

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

affiliations.org_name: University of South Florida - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: Firms whose turnover stays below a VAT threshold do not need to register for VAT, and many unregistered firms keep their turnover just below it. We measure how much more such firms grow when the threshold is raised, a question that arises whenever governments revise these thresholds. We study the 36 percent increase of Romania's VAT threshold in 2018, using the financial statements of all Romanian companies and their VAT registration histories. We compare the unregistered firms just below the old threshold with firms selected with the same rule in nine other years when the threshold did not change. After one and two years, the effect on their reported turnover is about 9 and 15 log points, concentrated among the firms closest to the old threshold. Both estimates exceed every estimate that the same comparison gives for years without a change. We also show that in Romania, a comparison used in earlier literature to measure growth held back by a VAT threshold would considerably overstate this effect.

detail.abstract: Retirees with individual accounts in Chile, Mexico, Peru and Colombia can keep their balance invested under programmed withdrawal or buy a life annuity. We ask whether an immediate real life annuity bought at 65 gives a higher risk-adjusted lifetime withdrawal (a downside-weighted certainty equivalent, relative risk aversion 3.12) than an author-defined spending band with a ratcheting floor, related to but distinct from US band rules. Contrasts, grids, the decision rule and a Holm adjustment were recorded in an author-maintained hash registry before any result on real data was computed, not as an independent pre-registration; public posting followed the start of computation by six minutes, and the annuity-versus-programmed-withdrawal contrasts re-judge results already seen. Each country uses its own 21-to 25-year sample and a long US robustness sample (1934-2026), 50,000 resampled paths each. In all eight main contrasts, with the band started at the annuity's first-year income or at 4.0%, the annuity came out ahead in both samples, in every registered sensitivity cell and in high-inflation and high-depreciation paths; Holm-adjusted p-values, conditional Monte Carlo quantities given the samples, pricing assumptions and yardstick, were below 10-38. No evaluated start rate on the registered grid from 3% to 9% let the band match the annuity, and the annuity stayed ahead down to a money's worth of 0.46-0.50 or, mostly, at 0.40, the grid's bottom. The yardstick gives no value to bequests: started at 4.0%, the band left a median of 0.30-1.04 times the starting balance. Posthoc robustness analyses are reported separately.

title: The American-Put Exercise Boundary Across the Near-Expiry Carry Transition

detail.abstract: In the Black-Scholes model, the exercise boundary of an American put has different near-expiry laws according to whether the continuous dividend yield q is below, equal to, or above the interest rate r. These fixed-carry laws do not describe the joint limit in which expiry approaches and the rates nearly balance. We determine the boundary profile inside the logarithmic transition window on the q > r side. With x = σ 2 τ denoting variance time, the window lies at log(q/r) x| log x|. A nonlinear history equation defines a canonical profile joining the positive-carry square-root law to the square-root-logarithmic law. We prove that the exact stopping boundary selects this profile, with log-boundary error O(√ x/| log x|) uniformly on compact sets of the refined transition coordinate and of positive dimensionless interest rates. The selection depends on information inherited from the full exercise history. Computations show slow approach to the limit and support a formal correction that reduces the finite-maturity discrepancy. The result explains the boundary geometry across the transition; practical comparisons also show where established approximations remain more accurate.

title: Who Pays for the Dream? Leverage, Dealer Intermediation and the Distribution of Retail CFD Losses
affiliations: University of Tehran

detail.title: Who Pays for the Dream? Leverage, Dealer Intermediation and the Distribution of Retail CFD Losses

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is an independent researcher and a private trader whose own live trading account has been publicly verified by a third-party service since 2022. detail.abstract: Retail foreign-exchange and contract-for-difference (CFD) trading is marketed as a route to financial independence. This paper asks a simpler question than whether the route works: when it does not, where does the money go? Starting from the accounting identity of a closed trading pool, I show that the aggregate result of retail clients is bounded above by zero before costs and is strictly negative after spreads, commissions and financing, so that the marketed outcome is arithmetically unavailable to the majority regardless of skill or psychology. Three institutional features then determine who receives what the majority pays. First, leverage: for a fully margined position the adverse move that exhausts equity is 1/L, so a 1:500 account is exhausted by a 0.2% move, a fraction of a normal day's range; the natural experiments of the 2010 U.S. leverage cap (Heimer & Simsek, 2019) and the 2021 Australian product intervention (ASIC, 2021) show that capping leverage cut high-leverage traders' losses by about 40% and aggregate retail net losses by about 91%, while reducing brokerages' operating capital, which identifies the loss as intermediary revenue. Second, dealer intermediation: a broker that internalizes client flow (B-book) earns the client's net loss, so the model is viable only if clients lose on net, and its prevalence is itself evidence about expected client outcomes. Third, introducer compensation: educators paid per lot or per spread share earn from client volume rather than client results, which aligns them with the dealer and, combined with the attribution mechanism of Rakhshani Pourfard (2026b), removes the last party with an incentive to question the method. Jurisdictional arbitrage concentrates the highest leverage and weakest protections on clients excluded from regulated venues. The paper derives testable implications, states policy conclusions consistent with the evidence, and gives a practical rule: size positions by risk, not by available leverage, and treat offered leverage as a signal about the counterparty rather than as a gift.

detail.abstract: CIDA (Civilizational Irreversibility Detection Architecture) was drafted in March 2026 as six instruments (SOLIS, VELA, NEXUS, AURORA, BIOS and ATLAS) that apply one stress-and-threshold equation to solar-geomagnetic infrastructure, oversight of AI systems, strategic supply chokepoints, climate tipping elements, ecosystem keystones and digital infrastructure, with a composite index, Ψciv. Its stated aim was not to predict disasters but to detect the loss of recoverability. This paper reports what happened when that formalization was tested. A published exploratory design document withdrew or downgraded the March claims and checked the mathematics by computation. This companion synthesizes five model-based audit reports (four nodes in a first round and a mathematical audit in a second) into 22 findings (8 critical, 11 major, 3 minor) and finds eight audit assertions mistaken, imprecise or only partly supported. The calculated results are as follows. Only one of six threshold modifiers is both direction-correct and bounded. The stress index is zero for a fully healthy and for a fully collapsed system. The composite, as a sum, reaches its non-return regime when every instrument stands at about 0.12. Three of six retrospective validation criteria demand a high index for events that recovered. The stress index can be computed as specified for only two of the six instruments. And none of the quantities defined measures recovery capacity, which is what the construct is about. Candidate repairs (corrected modifiers, a damage companion, and a monotone composite aggregator with analytically bounded amplification, whose monotonicity, regime consistency and amplification bound are proved analytically) are specified and not adopted. All CIDA-specific computational tests use synthetic inputs and design-stage assumptions. External source checks are factual corrections, not empirical validation of CIDA. No CIDA component has been validated on any real system or historical record. CIDA is not a forecasting model or a warning system. The paper was drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), whose earlier errors it corrects, and reviewed and approved by the author; the use of AI is disclosed in the Declarations.

detail.abstract: We ask how three decisions in a defined-contribution plan (the default investment path, the payout rule at retirement and plan cost) change a representative participant's probability of keeping a minimum standard of living, with designs, metrics and a pass rule recorded in an author-maintained hash registry before any result was computed. A candidate must beat its benchmark by at least 10 bp a year of return equivalent, with a 95% lower bound above zero, in both U.S. (from 1934) and global (from 1990) samples. A fixed 70%-equity default beat the average U.S. participant's mix by 28 bp (U.S.) and 29 bp (global), and a target-date glide could not be told apart from it. Plan-run withdrawal rules that aim at the target spending for life beat moving the balance to cash by 101 to 149 bp. This comparison is against an all-cash retirement benchmark and should not be read as the value of a specific plan service. The dynamic rule's lead is partly mechanical: its spending floor equals the living floor. Plan-cost differences moved outcomes about one-for-one. Contrary to registered hypotheses, the default-path gap exceeded 10 bp and a late partial annuity worsened outcomes. Limitations: overlapping samples, one participant, no held-out period and limited power ("not distinguishable" does not mean equal).

detail.abstract: This study examines how a common European aviation safety regulatory model is translated across sovereign military institutions. The European Military Airworthiness Requirements (EMARs), which are substantially derived from the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) civil aviation framework but implemented voluntarily by national military airworthiness authorities, provide a case of cross-domain regulatory transfer. A comparative documentary case study was conducted using EMAR and national regulatory texts from Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. Corresponding regulatory clauses were compared to identify additions, deletions and substitutions. Deviations were mapped to a product-behaviour-process (PBP) framework to distinguish implications for technical outputs, regulatory actors and oversight processes. Institutional theory was used to interpret the interaction between convergence around the common baseline and adaptation to nationally embedded governance arrangements. The findings reveal differentiated harmonisation. Product-related technical deviations are limited, while behaviour-related deviations principally affect competence, licensing, training and responsibility allocation. Divergence is greatest in process provisions and associated acceptable means of compliance and guidance material, where authorities adapt oversight practices, documentation requirements and administrative procedures to national defence structures. The results indicate that national authorities largely retain the technical content of the EMAR baseline while translating the organisational and procedural mechanisms through which safety assurance is produced. The study contributes to safety regulation research by showing that a common regulatory model can achieve technical convergence without procedural uniformity. Mutual recognition therefore depends not only on textual alignment, but also on procedural transparency and credible evidence of functional equivalence between national oversight arrangements.

title: Scaling Up Renewables While Building Korean Industry: Recent Policy Shifts and Challenges from a Resource Security Perspective
affiliations: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.title: Scaling Up Renewables While Building Korean Industry: Recent Policy Shifts and Challenges from a Resource Security Perspective

affiliations.org_name: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade
affiliations.preferred_name: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade

detail.abstract:
Renewable energy resource security turns less on fuel supply than on having an industrial base that can reliably manufacture and procure solar and wind power equipment and the materials and parts that go into it. Rather than electricity security, this paper focuses on the risk that heavy dependence on foreign suppliers and concentrated supply chains will constrain South Korea’s domestic production and technology base and narrow its economic security options.

In 2026 the government put forward long-term contracts, support for domestic production, and next-generation technology development, among other measures, but expanding deployment does not automatically translate into manufacturing investment in Korea. Nor is there yet an adequate framework for aligning item-by-item priorities and support instruments between deployment policy and industrial and resource security policy.

Predictable demand therefore needs to be created through annual bidding and ordering plans, and support needs to be differentiated: for solar, around the cell production base and competition in modules; for wind, around demonstration, certification, and building an operating track record. The core resources already designated should be linked to concrete instruments such as early warning, fi nance, and technology development, and costs should be managed together with the results in production and investment. The goal of policy is not a localization rate for its own sake but the retention, at a tolerable cost, of the production and technological capabilities needed to respond to supply chain shocks.

detail.abstract: Many theories in strategic management predict that when a firm's environment changes, the firm adjusts interdependent choices together. Separate difference-in-differences estimates for two such choices identify average responses but do not show whether the same firms adjust both. We show that independent responses, decision dependence, and common firm-level drivers can generate the same pair of average effects. To aid the separation process, we develop an excess joint response (EJR) statistic, equal to the share of treated firms that change both choices minus the share expected if the two responses were independent. We also provide versions for continuous outcomes and staggered treatment, and three extensions that examine heterogeneity, changes in dependence, and temporal ordering. Finally, we apply the statistics to four empirical settings, on inventor mobility and patenting, patent litigation, environmental regulation, and drug acquisitions, to illustrate how they can help improve inference about how firms respond to events.

title: Banking, Unbundling, and Abundance
affiliations: American University - Washington College of Law

detail.title: Banking, Unbundling, and Abundance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding

affiliations.org_name: American University - Washington College of Law
affiliations.preferred_name: American University - Washington College of Law

detail.abstract:
Proponents of “unbundling” banking look at the ways in which banks fail to serve consumers and threaten financial crises, and see a solution in non-banks providing pieces of banking’s deposit-taking, payments, and lending services. The argument goes that these unbundled pieces pose fewer risks than the full bundle of banking services, and so less regulation is required – and that once banking regulation gets out of the way, competition and innovation from non-banks will unleash benefits for the public.  In this sense, unbundling has much in common with the “abundance agenda,” which is based on assumptions that private sector innovation will trickle down benefits to the public once it is unshackled from regulations.  This Article, however, shows that these assumptions do not stand up to scrutiny in the banking context, and that unbundling is a Trojan Horse for deregulation that threatens the public interest.  

Economic incentives will encourage banking functions to be “rebundled” outside the regulatory perimeter by firms that share many of the vulnerabilities of banks, but with less regulation to address them.  Pressure to deregulate banks will also increase as banks face increased competition from firms subject to less regulation.  Money market mutual funds are the “patient zero” of this dynamic, but today it is most obviously playing out in the context of Silicon Valley fintech firms. Silicon Valley is characterized by the aggressive pursuit of monopolies, contempt for regulation and domain expertise, and an embrace of anti-democratic ideologies.  All of this should make us wary of handing over our nation’s financial infrastructure to fintech firms, The second Trump administration, however, has rushed to implement a plethora of regulatory accommodations for Silicon Valley fintechs.  These accommodations are likely to not only result in fintechs rebundling banking functions, but also in their bundling banking functions together with non-financial businesses in the form of vertically-integrated “everything apps.”  Instead of giving up on banks and hoping that the fintech sector will better serve the public, policymakers should focus their attention on forcing banking functions back into regulated banks, and then on legislative and regulatory reforms to make banks better.

detail.abstract: Studies of the gender pay gap during the Industrial Revolution mostly compare average earnings, wage rates or wage ratios at a given time, or use cross-sectional earnings by age to infer earnings growth over the life course. Few studies use firm-level wage books to follow the earnings of the same workers and examine who remained at the top of each department's earnings distribution. This paper uses the wage books of the Strutt mills from the first quarter of 1801 to the third quarter of 1804 to construct earnings trajectories within each department. It compares men's and women's earnings growth among trajectories with similar first normal weekly earnings and observation spans. It also examines how long men and women remained at the top of their department's earnings distribution. Earnings grew much faster among spinners and carders than among pickers. Women's earnings did not grow uniformly more slowly than men's across departments. Yet workers who remained at the top of their department's earnings distribution were almost all men, mainly those whose first normal weekly earnings were already high. The paper provides longitudinal evidence from within a firm on where gender inequality emerged along earnings trajectories in early factories.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we propose a new congressional advisory body, one designed for the Internet age: a Congressional Office of Science and Technology Analysis (COSTA). We focus particularly on how it would be organized and what kinds of work it would do. Our case for the COSTA is predicated on the conviction that it should have no agenda of its own other than to support Congress. Just as happened with the old OTA, other audiences—the executive branch, state and local government, private businesses, public-interest groups, and the press—would likely find value in the work of the new COSTA. But its success should be measured entirely in terms of the extent to which it is able to help committees and members of Congress to make informed decisions.

title: Does Deribit Lead? Cross-Exchange Price Discovery and the Limits of Retail Latency Arbitrage in Bitcoin and Ether Options

The study placed no live orders; all trading results are simulated paper trades on public market data.

detail.abstract: Deribit hosts the majority of open interest in bitcoin and ether options, and the option listings on Binance and Bybit are widely assumed to re-quote off it. If that re-quoting happens with a delay, a trader who watches Deribit could pick off stale quotes on the secondary exchanges. This paper tests the hypothesis end to end with public market data and a pre-specified sequence of four pass/fail gates: connectivity and market structure, the existence of a lead-lag relation, the feasibility of acting on it from a retail connection, and live paper trading net of realistic costs. A four-hour synchronized recording of 2.16 million quote and mark updates shows that the perpetual future, not Deribit, leads price discovery in short-dated at-the-money options; Binance and Bybit option quotes respond to the perpetual within 50-100 ms. Deribit's own quotes carry statistically significant incremental information (Driscoll-Kraay t = 3.5-6.3 and at least 2.6 under every alternative treatment of the panel dependence; circular-shift placebo p ≤ 0.005; the sample was extended after an underpowered pilot, so these levels are nominal), but its economic value is $0.29-1.06 per BTC contract against roughly $44-54 of retail fees and spread. A three-hour live paper-trading session and an 18-minute confirmation run on 56 options with latency-aware immediate-or-cancel fills produce 236,146 simulated trades, mean net losses of $20.76-$41.03 per trade across exchanges and holding periods, and four profitable trades. In the same two sessions a crossed-market strategy registers 197,866 crossed quote updates, none large enough to cover costs, so it executes no trades; these counts carry no quote-age check. In a separate replay of the four-hour recording, 44% of 141,344 crossed quote checks fail a quote-age and synchronisation filter. Of four follow-up designs, one was tested empirically-a full-chain cross scan, which finds only long-dated carry and minimum-tick artefacts-and one was given a preliminary feasibility check-Polymarket digital options priced off the Deribit smile, which deviate from fair by amounts within model error; settlement-window mispricing and maker-side quoting were assessed only as proposals and not tested. The paper documents the measurement pitfalls that generate false positives in this setting, most importantly the USD/USDT settlement mismatch, and releases all code.

detail.title: Quality Management System as a Strategy for Process Bottleneck Reduction: An Assessment of Three Selected Procedures in the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest regarding the conduct or writing of this research. Furthermore, no competing interests exist relevant to the content of this article.

detail.abstract: This study examined the implementation of selected Quality Management System (QMS) practices and their relationship with perceived process bottleneck reduction in three selected procedures of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR): Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN) Issuance, Processing and Issuance of Tax Clearance Certificate (TCC), and Processing and Issuance of the One-Time Transaction (ONETT) Computation Sheet (OCS)/electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR). Specifically, it assessed the implementation of QMS practices in terms of process standardization, process monitoring, risk-based thinking, corrective action, and continual improvement, as well as perceived process bottleneck reduction in terms of unnecessary process steps, processing and approval delays, duplication and rework, coordination delays, and clarity of process responsibilities. The study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design involving 23 BIR employees selected through total sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through frequency, percentage, weighted mean, standard deviation, and Spearman rank-order correlation. Findings revealed that selected QMS practices were highly implemented, obtaining an overall mean of 4.70, while perceived process bottleneck reduction also received a high assessment, with an overall mean of 4.54. Furthermore, correlation analysis revealed a statistically significant positive relationship between QMS prac tices and perceived process bottleneck reduction (ρ = 0.733, p = 0.000068). The null hypothesis was therefore rejected. The findings indicate that higher assessments of QMS implementation are associated with higher assessments of process bottleneck reduction. The study highlights the importance of strengthening quality management practices, particularly continual improvement and workflow streamlining, to support more efficient and responsive public service delivery.

detail.abstract: Using daily rental indices for Nvidia A100, H100 and B200 accelerators, this paper examines how GPU rents vary across generations and what that implies for depreciation and collateral value. The two older chips rent much closer to parity per kilowatt of power than per unit of throughput, and the two newer chips the reverse. Rent per kilowatt is nearly flat across older chips and rises steeply at the frontier, and the A100's rent per kilowatt mostly stays above a bound implied by replacement economics, consistent with a power-linked floor while energized capacity is scarce. A valuation model built on this pattern implies that an accelerator retains about 72%, 44% and 21% of its value after one, three and six years in the baseline. Matching a six-year booked life requires the floor to decline by about 3.4% a year or less, and a five-and-a-half-year life about 5.4% or less.

detail.abstract: Emotion recognizers are increasingly trained on texts generated by large language models, yet writers and readers often judge the emotion of the same text differently. Whether such recognizers reproduce this disagreement is unclear. In this study, we design an evaluation framework that separates the average tendency of each perspective from the direction and magnitude of text-level differences. Students trained on texts generated with writer or reader prompts are adapted with few human labels: paired text-label anchors, an unpaired label set, or a label distribution alone. A signature shift measures population-level differences, and a centered alignment and a magnitude ratio measure text-level ones. On a Japanese and an English corpus, perspective prompts did not transfer a consistent perspective, and a label distribution alone restored most of the population-level shift. Text-level differences remained hard to reproduce even with all labels or with direct training on the difference, and a better predictor of one perspective could worsen the difference. Reproducing human disagreement therefore requires evaluating text-level differences directly.

detail.abstract: Most theories of external financing predict debt, especially when financing needs are small. Incorporating entrepreneurial risk aversion into a standard moral-hazard model reverses this prediction: when the financing need is small, the entrepreneur is paid first, and levered equity -- the polar opposite of debt -- is approximately optimal among all limited-liability contracts. Debt leaves the entrepreneur bearing residual firm risk; this strengthens effort incentives, but the benefit is second-order when the amount raised is small, while risk sharing is first-order. For large financing needs, the investor is paid first and optimal financing includes debt. These results rationalize equity financing for start-ups and suggest greater use of equity-like financing in developing countries.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how status signaling shapes the diffusion of sustainable technologies. We develop an agent-based model that integrates two distinct forms of social status: conspicuous consumption, associated with traditional wealth-oriented prestige, and conspicuous conservation, reflecting the social value attached to visible sustainable choices. Heterogeneous consumers interact with strategically adapting firms that differentiate products along environmental and prestige dimensions. Calibrated to the German electric vehicles market, the model reproduces qualitative diffusion patterns and shows how diffusion accelerates when green innovations simultaneously signal material prestige and environmental values. The results further demonstrate how the effectiveness of this mechanism depends on structural conditions such as the income distribution and market structure.
