detail.abstract: Food waste in grocery retail arises both on store shelves and in consumers' homes, yet the growing adoption of buy-online-pickup in store (BOPS) can change how waste is generated across these two locations. We study how BOPS reshapes the effectiveness of two widely used waste-reduction interventions: grocers' investments in freshness technology and governments' per-unit waste taxes. We develop an analytical model comparing a store-only retailer with an omnichannel retailer that offers BOPS when profitable. In-store customers observe freshness before purchasing, whereas BOPS customers commit before fulfillment. Our main results are as follows. The profit and waste implications of freshness technology depend jointly on channel structure and the convenience of in-store shopping. When in-store shopping is convenient, the store-only retailer realizes a larger profit gain and reduces store waste, whereas the omnichannel retailer realizes a smaller profit gain and may experience increased store waste. When in-store shopping is inconvenient, both comparisons can reverse. A retail waste tax also creates a trade-off: it reduces store waste but increases household waste, potentially raising total waste when household spoilage is sufficiently high. Whether the BOPS option mitigates or amplifies this unintended effect depends on online convenience. When the online channel is relatively convenient, the tax-induced increase in total waste is no greater for the omnichannel retailer than for the store-only retailer; when the online channel is less convenient, this comparison can reverse. These findings show that waste interventions must be evaluated alongside retailers' channel structures and their effects on both store and household waste.

detail.abstract: Digital systems are reshaping how infrastructure organisations anticipate disruption, coordinate response and sustain performance under conditions of uncertainty. Yet organisational resilience is often explained either as a set of internal capabilities or as an outcome of technology adoption, with limited attention to the causal mechanisms through which technological change conditions resilience in complex socio-technical settings. This paper addresses this gap by empirically confirming and refining a mechanism-based model of Organisational Resilience (OR) in Australian infrastructure organisations. Grounded in critical realism, the study draws on 19 semi-structured interviews and 1,653 coded data segments to examine how activation conditions, digital enablers, generative mechanisms and outcome mechanisms interact during disruption. The findings confirm Collective Capability (CC), Adaptive Capability (AC) and Dynamic Capability (DC) as core generative mechanisms, while identifying Networked Coordination (NC) as an additional system-level mechanism. The analysis further clarifies Network Mobilisation (NM) and Informal Coordination (IC) as activation conditions that support cross-boundary and relational coordination. Digital enablers, including Artificial Intelligence (AI), Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), the Internet of Things (IoT), Big Data (BD) and Robotics, function as selective conditioning structures rather than direct drivers of resilience. Their resilience value depends on integration, governance, trust, interoperability and connection to organisational action. The paper contributes a critical realist explanation of how OR emerges through the interaction of organisational practices, digital systems, cross-boundary coordination and infrastructure governance. It advances a socio-technical understanding of resilience by showing how technological change reshapes the organisational and governance conditions through which infrastructure organisations activate, coordinate and sustain resilience capabilities across interdependent systems.

detail.abstract: This paper examines mergers and acquisitions (M&A) through the lens of biblical principles, focusing on the need to act in good faith at every step of the process, whether evaluating a target company, negotiating contracts, or onboarding after a merger. For Christian finance professionals, this approach goes beyond simple compliance; it is about upholding a standard that reflects Christ in our actions and interactions. When valuing a target business, diligence and fairness are essential, as an accurate valuation affects both sides and should be approached with honesty, as Gaughan (2017) notes. During contract negotiations, transparency is critical, especially when terms such as leveraged buyouts or collateralized assets are involved; unforeseen impacts can be minimized when all parties are informed and agreements are approached with respect. Onboarding presents its own challenges, particularly for personnel at the acquired firm. Acting in accordance with agreed terms, treating employees with grace, and ensuring clarity around roles can help establish trust. Scripture offers relevant guidance here, as 2 Kings 12:15 reminds us of the importance of honesty and Romans 12:10 calls us to show honor to others. Financial professionals who ground their practice in these values demonstrate that M&A is not merely about profit but about integrity, and they help set a higher standard for how business can and should be conducted.

detail.abstract: This paper compares Honeywell International Inc.’s shareowner letters and annual reports for fiscal years 2022, 2023, and 2024 to identify the changes, improvements, and deteriorations the company experienced during a period of leadership and structural transition. The most consequential changes were the succession from Darius Adamczyk, whose letters stressed the Accelerator operating system and organic growth, to Vimal Kapur, who became chief executive in 2023 and adopted a more narrative style, and the plan, announced between October 2024 and February 2025, to separate Honeywell into three independent, publicly traded companies in automation, aerospace, and advanced materials. Improvements include $4.2 billion of share repurchases and $2.7 billion of dividends in 2022, a 5 percent increase in research and development spending in 2024, nearly $9 billion of acquisitions in 2024, ESG commitments such as carbon neutrality in operations and facilities by 2035, and candid discussion of risk in management’s discussion and analysis. Deteriorations include the sales lost when Honeywell suspended and wound down its Russian operations in 2022, the execution risks of splitting the company during a leadership change, and exposure to interest rates, supply chains, and geopolitical uncertainty. Drawing on research on corporate spin-offs and ESG performance, the paper concludes that Honeywell is a company in transition whose strategy reflects resilience, adaptability, and ambition.

detail.abstract: My 2024 experiment found substantially higher joint gains when both negotiating parties had AI support than when only one or neither did. It did not measure trust or isolate the processes behind the gains. I revisit that pattern by asking when and how bilateral AI support could reduce the trust needed for integrative negotiation. The central proposal is that useful preparation could make particular integrative actions easier and less risky, allowing parties to attempt them with less interpersonal trust. I extend the Negotiation-AI Competence Matrix into a three-dimensional Negotiation-AI Capability Framework: negotiation expertise, AI literacy and tool strength. Applied to each party, it relates human capabilities to the knowledge and assistance supplied by the tool. Its distinctive concern is the recipient's ability to assess and develop a proposal, alongside the proposer's ability to construct it. Established low-trust bargaining tactics and earlier computer-assisted preparation provide the starting point. The framework distinguishes working with limited disclosure, sharing priorities while protecting sensitive limits, and trust developing through informed and responsive conduct. It yields predictions about reduced dependence on initial trust and the support each party needs. These are conceptual predictions, not mechanisms established by the 2024 study.

detail.abstract: This paper examines an authentic photograph selected and framed so as to stand for a broader political or moral reality. In April 2026, the cover of the Italian weekly L'Espresso concerning violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank, sought to make a particular photograph emblematic of the occupation. The photograph is not alleged to be fabricated, nor does this paper dispute the reality of violence committed by some settlers. The question is whether it is consistent with the limits of ethical journalism to select, crop, title, and circulate an authentic image in such a way that visible markers of Jewish religious identity become part of the representation of culpability. This paper proposes one underlying condition, systemic epistemic weakness, and three related concepts arranged on a spectrum: (i) iconographic extension of culpability, (ii) iconographic imprudence, and, at the strong end, (iii) representational discrimination. It proposes seven factors for assessing editorial choices of this kind and tests them against the strongest objection, that the identity markers are pertinent and necessary to the story. This paper does not infer antisemitic intent on the part of L'Espresso, it does not claim to demonstrate actual audience effects, and it locates the case at the level of imprudence. It identifies a representational risk arising when a true individual case resonates with an older repertoire of false collective stereotypes. The paper concludes that editorial responsibility concerns not only whether an image is true, but also whether it is liable to create amalgams and thereby consolidate false accusations against religious groups.

detail.abstract: We study admission and configuration control in reusable-resource loss networks, where customers may be rejected or assigned resource bundles that remain fixed until departure. In a high-volume regime with arrival rates and capacities proportional to $n$, we evaluate performance against a snapshot benchmark that optimizes allocation for each realized offered population. We develop virtual load control (VLC), a lightweight policy whose virtual records reproduce this population process pathwise. It achieves $O(\log n)$ snapshot-relative loss when a new structural condition, Local Support Completeness (LSC), holds and $O(\sqrt n)$ otherwise. A full-menu extension (FM-VLC) retains these guarantees while allowing regulated use of off-support configurations. The logarithmic bound is tight under an additional capacity-competition condition, and the square-root bound is tight whenever LSC fails. Numerical experiments illustrate the predicted loss regimes and strong finite-scale performance. Our work advances the analysis of stochastic resource allocation under degeneracy by distinguishing losses due to fluid averaging from those inherent in dynamic control.

detail.abstract: Entrepreneurship education provides with a range of well-established tools for designing and testing a proposed venture. Aspiring entrepreneurs also need disciplined ways to learn from ventures already operating in relevant industries. This paper presents the START Framework, which brings together three elements into a single structure: a five-stage research-to-action process (the core architecture); six research dimensions (the substantive questions that are investigated at each stage); and a C-I-P source classification (a provenance protocol applied throughout the process). START stands for Scan the Industry, Trace Startup Journeys, Analyze Startup Strategies, Review Evidence and Compare, and Transfer Learning. The six dimensions are Problem, Customers, Solution, Differentiation, Business Model, and Evidence & Risks. "C" is company claims, "I" is independent sources, and "P" is primary research that the researcher has collected themselves. The framework supports evidence traceability, cross-case comparison, context-sensitive interpretation, and designing tests for one's own venture. The paper sets out what the framework is, where it fits in the literature on market intelligence, opportunity recognition, organizational learning, and comparative case research, how it differs from other approaches, and provides an application protocol, research instrument, assessment rubric, testable propositions, and a validation agenda. It proposes the framework but provides no empirical validation of its effectiveness.

detail.abstract: Identity Load — the degree to which a brand surfaces through cultural rather than category-canonical retrieval channels — is a confirmed moderator of AI Presence: v1.6's H_IdentityLoad_Direct returned CONFIRMED on these substrates (v0.21 cosmetics Cell B IL-Direct δ = +7.12, 95% CI excluding 0; v0.22 automotive CONFIRMED; v0.20 skincare PARTIAL; v1.6, SSRN 6816340). This paper asks whether that same moderator governs a different component — cross-model Consistency, operationalized as the mean-independent dispersion instrument φ (higher φ = greater cross-model dispersion, i.e. lower consistency) — and finds that it does not. In a pre-registered, frozen re-analysis of the canonical two-channel trio (skincare, cosmetics, automotive; 72 brand units, 53 analyzable after the pre-specified true-zero/saturation partition), the pooled within-substrate rank association between continuous IL-Direct and φ is null: ρ = −0.008 (stratified permutation p = 0.955; n = 53, above the pre-registered power floor of 45). The test is powered, not silent: φ's mean-independence (|ρ(φ, recall-mean)| = 0.091) makes the raw association an inferential claim, and the surviving IL-Direct spread is real — the excluded units are the identity-load-neutral category staples. The orthogonality of an active Presence-side moderator to Consistency is positive evidence that the two components are governed by different mechanisms — the dissociation a two-component account of AI availability requires. The claim is deliberately bounded: a single moderator against a single consistency instrument is one dissociation result contributing to component-distinctness, not a proof of it.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether competition law can bear Article 43. Rights become real when a price meets a purse. A mother weighs insulin against maize flour. Constitutional doctrine watches the State while private sellers set the price. At that moment the market decides, not the Bill of Rights. The paper advances a thesis of load-bearing markets. A market is load-bearing when its failure denies the vulnerable essentials. Such markets demand enforcement of constitutional intensity. The thesis rests on a conversion channel between entitlement and access. Three arguments follow. First, private market power engages Article 20(1) and the State's dual role. Second, the Competition Act should be read on an essentiality gradient. Scrutiny rises as goods approach food, health, water and shelter. Essential inputs inherit essentiality from the goods they make. Dominance may arise from scarcity, not only from market share. Burden logic from Article 20(5)(a) then reaches dominant sellers of essentials. Third, merger approval is a State measure and must not retrogress. The paper tests these claims against institutions and evidence. Maize flour prices, medical inflation and the Carrefour decisions supply Kenyan evidence. South Africa's bread cartel, Dis-Chem and Health Market Inquiry supply comparison. The 2026 OECD peer review exposes thin enforcement capacity. Remedies remain procedurally fragile and regulators overlap. Counterarguments meet the thesis where they arise. They include price-control scepticism, the efficiency paradox and proportionality limits on property. The paper answers each with doctrine and data. It proposes rights-triggered market inquiries when essential prices outrun headline inflation. It also proposes rights impact statements for mergers in load-bearing markets. Together these moves reconcile markets with the Constitution's social promise. Competition law becomes a delivery mechanism for socioeconomic rights. It ceases to be a neutral referee. The 2 contribution is conceptual, doctrinal, empirical and practical. Kenyan courts and regulators can act now.

detail.abstract: Job seekers increasingly report applying to and interviewing for positions that do not exist or that employers are not planning to fill immediately. We refer to these advertised positions as "ghost jobs." Using a large language model, we construct a measure of ghost jobs from over two million Glassdoor interview reviews. We find evidence consistent with three strategic explanations: capital market signaling, information extraction, and talent hoarding. Ghost jobs are more prevalent when firms have incentives to convey growth to investors, obtain information from candidates, or build candidate pools before hiring needs are certain. Ghost jobs also generate negative spillover effects for both capital market participants and labor market peers. For capital markets, analysts who rely on big data and labor signals exhibit substantial declines in forecast accuracy for covered firms with reported ghost jobs. In addition, labor market peers subsequently hire fewer workers, form worse worker-job matches, and take longer to fill vacancies when focal firms post ghost jobs. Finally, ghost jobs impose costs on posting firms, as these firms receive less favorable employer ratings in the future. Overall, our evidence suggests that ghost jobs reduce the usefulness of labor demand disclosures to capital market participants and create frictions in labor market matching.

detail.abstract: Performance evaluations are intended to identify weak governments so they can be helped. The paper indicates that many of the weakest are missed by Indonesia's electronic-based government (SPBE) evaluation. In 2024, 102 of the 485 regencies and cities assessed had not been assessed in 2021. According to an official letter from KemenPAN-RB, 98 of them had not completed the self-assessment and were given a second chance, but they too did not complete it. The absent regions were poorer, smaller, and much more common in eastern Indonesia; there were none in Java. Three years on, they scored 0.87 points lower on the 1 to 5 scale than the regions assessed in the first stage. Even after adjusting for human development, poverty, population, internet use and location, the margin is still 0.23 to 0.28 points. Counting them, the share of regions classified Baik or better in 2024 decreases from 83% to 72% and the Java gap increases from 0.87 to 1.02 points. Non-participation is consequently an early warning signal not captured by standard statistics. It can be used by evaluators to focus support before scores are released.

title: Scientific Anti-Racism: The Economic Illusion of Racial Superiority

detail.abstract: Race is a social construct with real consequences, yet public discourse conflates observable group differences with innate racial hierarchy. This paper systematically refutes these claims through three approaches: philosophical analysis, computational evidence, and econometric demonstration. First, we show race is not a biological natural kind; machine learning clustering fails to recover human racial categories from facial features. Second, using cross-national data across six domains: national sentiment, athletic performance, measured intelligence, physical fitness investment, and appearance-related spending, we demonstrate that 32-65% of variation commonly attributed to race is explained by national income (GNI per capita, PPP). Third, we find that claims about physical appearance and culture track economic gradients reflecting resource differences and state capacity. These results indicate that perceived racial superiority reflects omitted variable bias: economic inequality misinterpreted as inherent group difference. We conclude that combating racism requires not denial of difference, but celebration of diversity alongside vigorous pursuit of economic equity.

detail.abstract: Can tax subsidies expand the geographic reach of startup investing? Despite decades of growth, venture capital (VC) remains concentrated in a handful of metropolitan areas, leaving most of the country with limited access to startup financing. We study the 2009-2010 enhancement of the Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS) program, which eliminated federal capital gains taxes on investments in qualifying startups. By raising the payoff to success, the reform made riskier investments more attractive, including entry into unfamiliar markets. This incentive is especially strong for VC funds. Relative to similarly sized metros that already had VC, the reform raised the probability that a previously unserved metro received VC investment in qualifying sectors by 8 to 10 percentage points. There was no comparable increase in sectors excluded from QSBS or among angel investors, who receive the same tax benefit. Startups in newly served markets performed like those in other non-hub markets, created high-wage jobs, and attracted scientific and technical workers, some from established hubs. Our findings suggest that a sufficiently large subsidy can extend VC into markets it had long bypassed, even with no requirement on where startups are located.

detail.abstract: We are today in the early stages of the superintelligence economy. When intelligence is industrialized, and so becomes cheap and abundant, value moves to its complements. A superintelligence economy has two prime factors: intelligence and tacit knowledge embedded in local context. We can model growth as the automation of tasks, but because tasks are gross complements, AI substitution into one task moves the constraint to whatever AI cannot yet supply. These constraints, or bottlenecks, slow the speed at which AI diffuses through the economy, and so the rate of growth. They also become the new sources of value and advantage. We draw attention to three. First, tacit knowledge: local expertise that AI cannot yet economically acquire or reproduce; it shows up as taste, judgment and verification. Second, cooperation and authority: who has the authority to act, who is trusted, and who is held accountable when things go wrong. Third, demand, where consumers are willing to pay for human involvement in the products and services they buy. Each bottleneck can earn its owner a rent, and market dynamics incentivize its removal or replacement. This race sets the pace of the transition and shapes how the gains are distributed. Economic strategy and policy should focus on bottlenecks: owning those a country or firm holds and removing those that limit it. AI creates value at three positions: supplying inputs, making models, and using models. Use is likely the largest source, and the main path for most countries, including Saudi Arabia and New Zealand.

detail.abstract: We compare a pairwise ranking objective (LambdaRank) with a pointwise squared-error objective for selecting a concentrated long-only portfolio from the Indonesia Stock Exchange, holding features, purged walk-forward folds, targets, universe and trading rules fixed and tuning each objective separately. Theoretically, the population optimum of the regression objective is the conditional mean of the rank target, whereas the NDCG-optimal ordering is a geometrically weighted tail-probability index that rewards dispersion; the two coincide under first-order stochastic dominance and can disagree otherwise. A Gaussiancopula attenuation law links whole-sample and top-slice information coefficients and supplies a falsifiable benchmark. Empirically (2018-2025, costs of 25/35 bps), the data do not show that ranking dominates regression: top-quantile IC is 0.051 (regression) versus 0.043 (LambdaRank), p = 0.33; Sharpe ratios tie at the tuned seed (1.34 vs. 1.34) but are 1.41 vs. 1.16 averaged over 20 seeds, with a seed-paired gap of-0.25 whose 95% interval [-0.90, 0.44] includes zero. LambdaRank behaves as a top-slice instrument: negative IC outside the top bucket, higher precision@20, twice the volatility, a market beta of 1.27 and a momentum loading, and a return advantage concentrated after mid 2024. An equalweight blend has the best Sharpe ratio (1.45). Seed noise is of the order of the effect size, and survivorship in the free data source is the main caveat. This is a working paper, a revised version using point-in-time data and a cross-market replication is forthcoming.

detail.abstract: Social-commerce platforms such as TikTok and Instagram offer both video content and online shopping, earning revenue from two sources: sellers' ad spend and commissions on product sales. We focus on the problem of managing these revenue sources and develop a game-theoretic model in which a platform allocates organic (free) viewer traffic across sellers that differ in product quality, anticipating that this will incentivize investments in ad-content engagement and influence purchases of paid viewer traffic. Our analysis and results unveil several important insights. First, organic traffic strengthens sellers' incentives to produce more engaging content, thereby raising the return on every paid impression and inducing additional paid-tra"c purchases. Second, the optimal allocation of organic traffic is non-monotonic in product quality. In particular, the lowest-quality sellers receive no traffic, and their viewer segments are redirected to the top seller. Among the remaining sellers, intermediate-quality sellers therefore receive the least organic traffic: the platform allocates organic traffic to low-quality sellers to encourage paid traffic purchases, and to high-quality sellers that generate commission revenue. Third, more accurate prediction of viewer preferences may not translate into higher platform profits because it improves high-quality sellers' options and weakens the incentive role of organic traffic.

detail.abstract: This descriptive working paper asks how subscription pricing structures and AI feature access differ across selected email productivity software products. We recorded 30 plan listings from 12 vendors' own pricing pages in a hand-picked sample, rechecked on 31 October 2026. Headline statistics use the 24 verified plans from 10 vendors, excluding 6 plans whose prices could not be verified. Among 14 annual-billing plans priced in US dollars, list prices run from $4.17 to $64.00 per seat per month (median $25.00); monthly and two-year plans are reported separately. Where both terms are printed, annual billing is priced 20.0 percent below monthly billing at the median (11 plans, 5 vendors). Of the 24 plans, 16 are coded as stating AI functionality, most often metered by credits or quotas (8) or included without a stated limit (5); 2 offer AI only as an add-on or integration and 4 do not state AI either way. No adjacent-tier pair meets the conditions for reading a price step as the price associated with AI access, so no AI price premium is computed; this is a finding about comparability. The analysis is exploratory and not pre-registered, and it makes no causal, welfare or representativeness claim. The author's company sells one of the products in this category and publishes the commercial price index from whose records the sample was drawn; its own product is excluded from the sample, and the vendors were not consulted.

detail.abstract: This article develops a conceptual framework for analyzing long-run economic interdependence between South Africa and Namibia when some of the conditions that drive it cannot be observed directly. The framework takes a methodological cue from the hidden-variable debate in quantum foundations, which sharpened three questions that also matter in economics: what an unobserved state must do to earn a place in a model, when a joint process can be treated as two independent ones, and how the conditions of measurement relate to what is measured. The model itself is a standard state-space model. Its starting point is a regional puzzle: South Africa and its neighbors are densely linked, yet econometric studies find little evidence of real growth spillovers from South Africa after 1994 once global shocks are controlled for. The framework treats linkage, spillover, and synchronization as distinct, and allows the strength of transmission through a given linkage to depend on latent conditions. Its central construct, systemic fatigue, takes two forms: production-side fatigue, which weakens an economy's capacity to convert inputs into outcomes, and measurement-side fatigue, which weakens what statistical systems record. The two cannot be separated using measured output alone, and measurement problems can make the two economies appear either more or less closely linked than they are. GDP per capita growth and the Human Development Index (HDI), the latter through its shortfall from the maximum, are modeled jointly. Fatigue lowers the effectiveness of conventional transmission channels, while alternative routes-knowledge networks, regional value chains, logistics, renewable energy, digital services, and institutional learning-may bypass bottlenecks. The paper closes with testable propositions, 1 Amavilah Latent States and Systemic Fatigue each paired with a falsification condition, and a research design. It makes no empirical claims.

detail.abstract: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 replaced a fragmented regime of debt recovery tribunals, company-court winding up and the Sick Industrial Companies Act with a single, time-bound process for corporate debtors. This book examines the two processes the Code provides for companies, the corporate insolvency resolution process and liquidation, as the statute, the regulations of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India and the decisions of the National Company Law Tribunal, the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal and the Supreme Court have shaped them in the Code's first years. It begins with the economics of insolvency, because the design choices of the Code, from the creditor-in-control model to its strict timelines, make sense only against the problems of collective action and value destruction that insolvency law exists to solve. It then follows a case from admission and withdrawal through the moratorium, the appointment and duties of the resolution professional, the verification of claims, the decisions of the committee of creditors and the eligibility of resolution applicants under section 29A, to the approval of a resolution plan. Where resolution fails, the book turns to liquidation, covering the appointment of the liquidator, the liquidation estate, the treatment of claims, the waterfall of distribution and dissolution, and the avoidance of preferential, undervalued and extortionate transactions. Throughout, it asks whether the tribunals and courts have kept faith with the purpose of the Code, and where they have not, it says so.

detail.abstract: This study examines how mobile commerce may support market access among micro and small enterprises in the Philippines, with particular attention to domestic expansion and cross-border e-commerce. It aims to identify the opportunities, barriers, and conditions associated with mobile-enabled business activities. The study employs qualitative content analysis of secondary sources, including peerreviewed journal articles, Philippine government publications, international organization reports, and credible industry-related publications. The findings indicate that social media, mobile applications, and online marketplaces provide potential channels for product promotion and customer acquisition. Philippine statistics also demonstrate substantial participation in online buying and selling activities and growing use of digital payments. Research on Philippine enterprises indicates that the benefits of digitalization may depend on business maturity, while international studies highlight the importance of technological, marketing, and operational capabilities. The study concludes that mobile commerce can provide opportunities for wider market access, but its effectiveness depends on connectivity, digital skills, transaction security, fulfillment capacity, and export readiness. The findings are limited by the scope and quality of the available secondary evidence.

detail.abstract: Interpretability research often explains the behavior of large language models (LLMs) through the concepts encoded in their internal representations, and a dimension that is more prominent in an internal representation is often assumed to matter more for behavior. However, it remains unclear whether representational magnitude predicts how sensitive a decision is to a dimension when several dimensions coexist in one internal state. This study develops a causal gain analysis framework that separates representational magnitude from causal gain, defined as the causal effect per unit magnitude. Two dimensions of an emotional state, its valence and the option it supports, are crossed in a factorial design of paired prompts. Their contrasts are extracted once from the residual stream and added back in both directions at the question tokens. The same vectors are then read out under an action question and an evaluation question. The framework also estimates a local gain from the output gradient and maps the contrasts across model families. Experiments on seven instruction-tuned LLM families showed that valence was about one order of magnitude larger than the action dimension in the representation and also had the larger raw effect on the choice. Per unit magnitude, however, the choice was more sensitive to the action dimension, and the evaluation question reversed this ordering. The reversal appeared in every family, in the local gradient, with each model's own vectors, and with answer formats without valence words. Vectors transferred from other families carried only a small part of the natural effect but reproduced the same ordering. These results show that representational magnitude does not predict decision sensitivity, whose relative ordering instead changes with the decision being made.

detail.abstract: Electricity is a shared input to three rapidly expanding forms of production: artificial intelligence (AI) computation, cryptocurrency mining, and the extraction and processing of minerals. Public debate compares these activities by headline electricity prices or by single quoted production costs, such as a "cost per bitcoin." This paper shows that such comparisons are not merely imprecise but structurally misleading, and it supplies the corrections. We begin from the identity that electricity cost per unit of output is the product of the electricity price and the electricity intensity of a defined output unit, and we embed that identity in a properly specified unit cost function. Four results follow. First, the elasticity of unit cost with respect to the electricity price equals the electricity cost share, and concavity of the cost function in prices makes the first-order approximation an upper bound on unit cost at every alternative price. Second, the ratio of the electricity price to value added per kilowatt-hour, P e /π e , is an exact, unit-free, and empirically measurable index of electricity sensitivity that is comparable across heterogeneous outputs, and production is viable in the short run if and only if this ratio does not exceed unity. Third, when ore grade affects milling energy and metallurgical recovery, the elasticity of mineral energy intensity with respect to grade is bounded above in absolute value by the naive estimate, giving a sign restriction that can be tested. Fourth, because bitcoin difficulty adjusts to free entry, cheap electricity is capitalised into difficulty rather than into a lower cost per coin: only relative, not absolute, electricity prices determine miner rents, so the standard comparative static fails for this sector alone. Illustrative calculations, labelled as modelled scenarios throughout, place bitcoin and primary aluminium at P e /π e of roughly 0.5-0.6 under central assumptions, against about 0.05 for AI computation and refined copper-an order-of-magnitude separation that survives wide parameter variation. We set out a regional design covering Africa, Asia, North America, Europe, and South Africa, a standardised unit system for twenty extractive commodities, five testable propositions, and an identification strategy that avoids the tautology latent in regressing an accounting identity on one of its own factors.

detail.abstract: The Decoupling Sovereignty Index (DSI) requires field data from places where formal sovereignty has weakened and conspicuous research can be dangerous. This paper establishes a field-research methodology for gathering such data through the Tri-Tiered Approach, the Visual Assimilation Protocol and the Deep Institutional Immersion Protocol. It examines the particular ethical challenges arising when deep immersion requires a researcher to operate under a borrowed identity, creating three obligations: the persona must be disciplined, the exit must be designed before entry, and the deception must be ethically justified. It proposes four tests-necessity, proportionality, protection and accountability-alongside rules for three difficult field situations and explicit duties to both the people observed and the researcher.

detail.abstract:
On September 4, 2026, the Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service proposed regulations entitled Racial Nondiscrimination in Private Schools (REG-119986-25). The proposal would deny tax-exempt status to any private school adopting a policy or practice that discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin “for any purpose,” and would delete the provisions of Revenue Procedure 75-50 that have authorized private schools to adopt minority-favoring admissions and financial assistance programs since 1975.

These comments, filed with Treasury and the IRS, argue that the proposed regulations exceed the agency’s authority and fail the requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act. They assemble the administrative record the rulemaking would reverse: a Treasury regulation in force since 1959, a 1972 regulation treating a private foundation’s ethnic-minority scholarship program as consistent with section 501(c)(3), ten published revenue rulings issued between 1967 and 1977, six memoranda of the Office of Chief Counsel, provisions of Revenue Procedure 75-50 the Service expressly retained in 2019, two determinations concerning the same school twenty-four years apart, and a private letter ruling issued nine months after Students for Fair Admissions. The preamble to the proposed regulations engages three items in that record.

The comments argue that Bob Jones University v. United States conditioned the Service’s authority on the sustained convergence of all three branches; that the common law of charitable trusts, from which section 501(c)(3) draws the meaning of “charitable,” distinguishes invidious exclusion from remedial inclusion; that the proposed regulations reverse six decades of the agency’s own position without acknowledgment or explanation; and that the rulemaking is arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act.

detail.abstract: Drawdowns, peak-to-trough losses in portfolio value, are what investors experience most directly. However, conventional risk measures provide limited insight into their depth, duration and recovery. This research examines historical drawdowns, develops a parsimonious model of drawdown dynamics, and introduces a practical framework for managing drawdowns as they unfold. Using a century of South African equity returns and half a century of bond returns as empirical case study, we document the severity and persistence of drawdowns and the importance of adverse-return clustering. Recovery typically takes longer than the initial decline, while drawdown depth alone does not predict above-average forward returns. In particular, the profitability of buying at the trough relies on a look-ahead premium unavailable in real time. A two-state Markov-switching autoregressive model captures the distributional and time-series properties of returns. Relative to geometric Brownian motion, it generates deeper maximum drawdowns at comparable Sharpe ratios, particularly in the tails. The starting regime also affects short-horizon drawdown risk, while the filtered volatile-regime probability provides a useful indicator of market stress. Finally, we introduce the recovery frontier, the probability of returning to a previous high within a given horizon based on current drawdown depth and Sharpe ratio. Combined with an investor-specified threshold, it provides a practical framework for deciding whether to maintain, reduce or hedge investment exposure.
